items.title: Immersive physical activations and AI powered experiences: last week's most read retail technology articles
items.summary: Check out our most clicked retail technology articles from last week, including Azoma, Westfield Rise, Lionsgate, Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Foot Locker, Stylitics, Co-op, Five Below, poq, Firstwork, and the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.Agentic commerce platform Azoma raises $11.2 million
items.body:
Check out our most clicked retail technology articles from last week, including Azoma, Westfield Rise, Lionsgate, Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Foot Locker, Stylitics, Co-op, Five Below, poq, Firstwork, and the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
Agentic commerce platform Azoma raises $11.2 million in Series A round led by Puma Growth Partners
AI shopping agents startup, Azoma, has announced a $11.2 million Series A funding round led by Puma Growth Partners, with participation from dunnhumby, Twin Path, MaRS IAF, Rank Ventures and Ignite Ventures and Angels from Google DeepMind and Legora.
The round will fund the expansion of Azoma's platform across the AI personal assistants space such as ChatGPT Dots and Meta Muse; as well as the build out of its optimisation and attribution capabilities for enterprise consumer brands utilising dunnhumby data.
The cash will also support team growth with a particular focus on recruiting AI talent. Azoma works with consumer brands including L'Oréal, Unilever, Mars, Beiersdorf and Reckitt. The round follows a $4 million seed announced in December 2025.
Azoma was founded in 2022 by Max Sinclair, a former Amazon executive; and Timur Luguev, a PhD and Postdoctoral Researcher in machine learning. Sinclair comments: "Three hundred and fifty million people used Alexa for Shopping last year. Walmart customers who use their AI shopping assistant Sparky spend 40% more than those who don’t."
"Instinct, the personal AI Assistant that launched in August with zero marketing budget, already accounts for $1 billion in transactions, and is growing at a rate of 10% day over day. Agent-to-agent commerce has arrived faster than anyone expected. For our customers, this will be more transformational than the internet. Agentic commerce will be on a par with how electrification birthed or transformed these enterprise consumer brands."
John Lewis, Asda, Morrisons, H&M, Dunelm, and Waitrose among 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards finalists
We're hugely pleased to present the finalists and shortlists for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards, sponsored by 3D Cloud, Business France, and Retail Technology Show 2027. We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! It’s now over to our star studded judging panel who will decide the winners to be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.
Click here to book your place at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony on Wednesday, 4th November.
Westfield Rise and Lionsgate launch Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping immersive experience in London
Westfield Rise, the in-house retail media agency of Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield (URW), has partnered with Lionsgate to launch The Hunger Games: The Capitol Experience, an exclusive immersive activation at Westfield London. Running from 30th October to 23rd November, the free ticketed experience will give fans the chance to step into the world of Panem ahead of the release of the movie.
Located in The Atrium at Westfield London, it will feature a Cornucopia installation, interactive moments inspired by the film, exclusive collectibles and a world exclusive film clip available only to visitors attending the activation. The activation forms part of Lionsgate’s wider campaign for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, which the studio has described as its largest above the line campaign of 2026, spanning TV, VOD, outdoor, social, digital, radio, PR, influencer and brand partnership activity.
Westfield will support the campaign through its owned marketing channels, including social media, CRM, digital platforms, editorial content, in-centre media and ticketing communications. The partnership also extends across URW's Northern European portfolio.
Supporting activity at Westfield Täby Centrum and Westfield Mall of the Netherlands will help amplify the campaign through local marketing, social content and customer communications. Additional campaign activity will also take place at Westfield Chodov in Prague.
Co-op and Devon & Cornwall Police double retail crime cases solves with new reporting system roll-out
The partnership, according to those involved, delivers significantly faster justice for offences carried out, with data from Devon & Cornwall Police showing crimes reported through the platform - which is called SentrySIS - achieving a solve rate of almost 60%, which is approaching double the force’s average solve rate for retail crime versus retail crime being reported by those using traditional channels.
Data from Devon & Cornwall Police also revealed that 90% of identified shop theft offenders are repeat offenders, with just 50 individuals responsible for around a quarter of all shop theft offences in the Devon and Cornwall force area, often with more than 100 known offences each.
The new system enables stronger intelligence sharing; improved tracking of repeat offenders - connecting multiple offences committed by the same individual and building stronger cases against prolific offenders and, closer collaboration with police both at a local and central level.
Store colleagues upload incident details, CCTV, photos and impact statement enabling police to record and allocate the crime in as little 30 minutes - a process that could take police up to seven days.
Furthermore, it removes the need for investigating officers to then approach the retailer for evidence, saving time for retailers and resulting in the average time taken for investigations to be completed and assigned an outcome being slashed by more than a third to 35 days.
The success of the pilot has seen the SentrySIS system, which links to Co-op’s wider partnership working with UK Partners Against Crime (UKPAC), now activated across all Co-op stores in Devon and Cornwall, with discussions now underway with additional police forces. Co-op’s own retail crime levels are falling with the retailer expected to see its lowest levels since the pandemic.
Foot Locker teams with Stylitics as retailer taps AI technology to launch app-based closet builder solution
Foot Locker has developed, in partnership with Stylitics, a new AI powered closet builder, Fits, within its mobile app. In a LinkedIn post,
Michael Cera, Interim Head of Product Management and Design at Foot Locker, said: “AI is everywhere. But, at Foot Locker, we challenged ourselves to think about how to improve and make positive change to our customers shopping experience through the use of AI.”
He added: “We engaged with customers, really listened, and in partnership with Stylitics, developed a key new closet builder within the Foot Locker app - let me introduce you to Fits! Start with something you own. Discover personalised outfits built around it. See those looks come to life on a virtual model.”
Customers can upload or take a photo of something they own, discover complete outfits built around it, and visualise those looks on a virtual model. Paired with a cart addition from the model view, the aim is to make purchasing a whole outfit styled around your own products that much easier.
Cera concluded: “This was a collaborative effort across Experience Design, Product Management, E-comm, Brand, and Stylitics, and came to life exactly as we all set out to do. Download or open your Foot Locker app today and give it a try!”
Ikea stumps up £31.5 million as it looks to make UK fulfilment more efficient and reduce packaging waste
Ikea UK is investing £31.5 million across its Peterborough and Doncaster customer distribution centres (CDC) as the retailer aims to make online fulfilment more efficient and sustainable.
In Peterborough, new technology is packaging customer orders to size and reducing material usage by up to 30%, by preventing waste from oversized boxes and filling paper. In Doncaster, Ikea is trialling a new regional fulfilment capability, serving customers in the north and Scotland from a closer location to them.
The investments will strengthen Ikea’s UK fulfilment network as online sales account for 43.3% of total UK sales in financial year 2026. It is investing £30 million in new technology for its Peterborough CDC, with the upgrades taking place over a two-year period. As part of this, it has launched new PackSize technology to prevent waste from oversized cardboard boxes and filling materials by packaging customer orders to size. On average, the technology reduces material usage by up to 30% and void fill by up to 60%.
The technology is expected to increase the share of parcels processed through automation at the Peterborough CDC from 47% today to 75% in 2027, helping the fulfilment team prepare orders for delivery more efficiently. These additional orders would otherwise have been packaged by manually creating a packing carton which includes having to measure the article then creating the cartons to fit the order. Three drones and nests were introduced at the site in January to support inventory management. They scan each aisle in short cycles, helping Ikea to keep stock in the right place and meet customer demand.
Ikea is investing £1.5 million in trialling a new fulfilment capability at its Doncaster CDC. The site now fulfils orders for customers in the Gateshead, Edinburgh and Glasgow areas, with plans for Sheffield to follow. By fulfilling these orders from Doncaster rather than Peterborough, Ikea expects to reduce emissions from delivery journeys by an estimated 280 tonnes of CO2 annually. The new capability has created an additional 80 jobs at the Doncaster site.
US retailer Five Below taps poq platform for launch of new native iOS and Android mobile apps
poq has announced the launch of new native iOS and Android mobile apps for Five Below. Tiffany D’Amato, Vice President of Digital, Five Below, comments: “Our customers live on their phones, and these apps give them a faster, more engaging way to experience everything they love about Five Below.”
“Partnering with poq allowed us to bring that vision to life quickly and effectively, with a truly native experience built for our shoppers. We’re confident these apps will drive stronger customer engagement and long-term growth for the brand.”
Helen Slaven, Chief Revenue Officer at poq, says: “Five Below is exactly the kind of brand app commerce was made for, with a huge, engaged customer base and a shopping experience built on discovery. We are thrilled to partner with them to turn mobile into an owned channel that retains customers, grows lifetime value and scales with the business.”
A built-in price scanner lets shoppers scan an item in store and check its price and details on the spot, while personalised search helps customers explore the various products Five Below has to offer. Store aware features surface the nearest store and stock availability and push notifications, keep customers close to new arrivals and seasonal drops. The apps are built on poq’s platform and integrated with the Five Below commercetools commerce stack.
Firstwork secures $15 million Series A as startup looks to scale applied AI for frontline workforce ops
Firstwork, an AI platform for frontline workforce operations, has announced a $15 million Series A led by Earlybird Venture Capital, with participation from Legion VC, Deel Ventures and existing investors Gradient and Y Combinator. The round brings its total funding to date to $20 million.
Firstwork was founded in 2024 by Vardhan Kapoor and Shubham Choudhary. Kapoor previously led APAC at Remitly and strategy at Deliveroo Singapore, while Choudhary was a Director of Engineering at Deel after helping build Rippling’s global employment infrastructure.
More than 150,000 frontline workers now start work through Firstwork each month. Customers including Deel, Job&Talent, Relay, Wonolo and BGSF have cut the time workers and HR teams spend on each new hire by up to 90%, according to the company.
“The systems employers rely on were built to record what happened, not to actually do the work,” says Kapoor. “That leaves HR and operations teams spending enormous amounts of time chasing documents, coordinating across systems and supporting workers through processes that extend well beyond day one. Applied AI changes what is possible."
"We can now give every frontline worker the kind of support that used to be reserved for the top of the labour market, from the moment they apply through every stage of their employment.”

items.body:
Towards the end of the 1970s, the brief but spectacular career of those punk rockers and folk devils the Sex Pistols was followed by The Great Rock’n’Roll Swindle, a rather tawdry drama-documentary. It recast their rise and fall as a huge scam, summed up by a slogan on a T-shirt worn by their former manager Malcolm McLaren: “Cash from Chaos”.
Back then, that motto was a neat representation of his personal brand of cultural mischief. But the culture always takes unexpected twists and turns – and 50 years on, an almost-identical maxim seems to be defining the fate of an increasing chunk of the British retail economy. While Andy Burnham pledges to restore life to town centres, a private equity outfit is busy buying up national retail chains and then shutting down scores of their outlets, while seemingly operating in line with its boss’s most celebrated quotation: “Where there’s chaos, there’s opportunity.”
Those words came from Jamie Constable, the owner of a set of businesses that includes Modella Capital, which specialises in “distressed investing” and “aggressive restructuring”. In 2024, Modella bought the craft supplies chain Hobbycraft – insisting on its “real commitment to bricks-and-mortar retail”, but then shutting 18 shops and triggering 600 job losses, while leaving redundancy costs to the taxpayer. Months later, it acquired the discount outlets branded as The Original Factory Shop, only for the entire chain to collapse. But its most ambitious move was its recent purchase of the 480 high-street shops that previously traded as WH Smith, rebranded by Modella as TG Jones (a completely made-up name, which it said would “keep that sense of a family business”), and the rapidly announced closure of up to 150 of them.
In September, 19 branches breathed their last, in such varied locations as Bath, Southend, Cardigan, Redhill and the Essex new town of Basildon. This month, the shutters are permanently falling in – among 23 places – Pinner, Truro, Inverness and Leek in Staffordshire. Thanks to their shortsighted folding into previous WH Smith premises, the closure plan will inevitably mean the loss of many local post offices: by early 2027, 70 will have gone. It will inevitably accelerate the decline of printed newspapers. But for me and many others, the key tragedy in this story is all about magazines, those gloriously tactile creations that played a crucial role in making many of us who we are.
I say that as someone who fell in love with this form of publishing as a child, via a weekly educational magazine called Look and Learn – stuffed, as I recall, with comic-strip versions of Dickens stories, and stuff about space exploration. By my early teens, I was an avid reader of Sounds, the Melody Maker and NME, the so-called weekly music papers that were really magazines whose ink came off on your fingers. Much to my amazement, between my 19th and 26th birthdays, I ended up successively working for all three – until, in 1995, I joined the now defunct company Emap Metro, which set enormous store by its mastery of glossy fortnightlies and monthlies.
Some of these names may mean precious little to younger readers, but spark a Proustian rush among older ones: Q, Smash Hits, Select (which I edited for three years), Sky, the metal and hard rock title Kerrang!, Big, Neon, FHM. Most have now closed, but three of the old stable are still standing, under different ownership: Kerrang!, which mostly lives online; the film bible Empire; and Mojo, the lovingly produced music magazine that I am thrilled to still write for.
Thirty years ago, we all knew that there was no better medium for in-depth interviews, or high-end photography. The management constantly asked us who our intended reader was, and what the future was likely to entail. Even the smallest cover-lines were pored over, as if the mere mention of Placebo or DJ Shadow might attract scores of newbies. And though a lot of us didn’t listen, we were told to never, ever put our magazines in sealed plastic bags (which, in line with a longstanding convention, would contain “free gifts”), for fear of losing the kind of punter who liked to browse before they bought.
And therein lies the TG Jones tragedy. The business has rightly acquired an utterly grim reputation, but is – or was – one reliable place to still find shelves full of printed content worthy of endless curiosity. And now? The culturally omnivorous twentysomething in Rickmansworth will no longer chance upon the latest edition of the cutting-edge music monthly the Wire, and thereby be inducted into a world of esoteric electronica and contemporary avant-garde jazz. The student-age customer in Ormskirk tiring of production-line pop may know nothing of the more substantial music covered by Mojo’s excellent competitor Uncut.
Would-be radicals will be unable to browse the printed iteration of Tribune; film freaks may be completely unaware of the in-depth, art-house wonders of Sight and Sound. Publishers will fall over themselves to alert us to subscription offers, but for a lot of people, they will be prohibitively expensive.
As George Orwell once put it, the UK is “a nation of stamp-collectors, pigeon-fanciers, amateur carpenters, coupon-snippers, darts-players, crossword-puzzle fans”. Products that reflect that enduring aspect of our national character are still at the core of magazine publishing, and why some titles still sell enviably: at the last count, for example, BBC Gardeners’ World sold a monthly average of 164,807 copies, while Country Living shifted 107,596. The broad women’s and fashion sector is also still here. It isn’t all over, by any means.
Still, one can easily imagine a Mark Zuckerberg-esque voice scoffing at all this as so much stone-age nonsense, and claiming that what printed magazines deliver can easily be either replicated or superseded on the internet. Experience often suggests otherwise: witness the fate of the once-independent online music magazine Pitchfork, bought out by the corporate publisher Condé Nast in 2015 and bizarrely folded into the workings of the men’s title GQ nine years later: a classic case of what we now know as enshittification. But there is an even bigger point here about how we now engage with the things we like and love, summarised in a forthcoming book titled Circulation: How Culture Moves in the Age of Algorithm by the Nashville-based US music insider David Macias, with a foreword written by Dan Clancy, the CEO of the livestreaming platform Twitch.
His argument is about music, but its logic applies across the cultural, recreational and sporting board. “The algorithm is great at finding me new music in the limited style I listen to,” he writes. “But it is really bad at showing me something new and different. My listening has become homogeneous, even though I can pick any album ever created.” This is the tedious prospect that the demise of the magazine will only accelerate – so after the high-street chaos has died down, we could be faced with an awful silence, broken only by the leakage from headphones playing the same things over and over again. And to speak the language of the insatiable capitalist, where will anyone find money in that?
- John Harris is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Retail leads the way on paternity leave as government urged to improve offer
items.summary: M&S and Tesco are among employers offering six weeks, highlighting gap with construction and agriculture “Being able to take six weeks’ paid paternity leave, flexibly, made a huge difference to me and my family, giving me the time to support my partner and settle into being a new parent,” said Marks & Spencer employee Joe Erskine. The food and clothing retailer increased its paternity leave offering from two to six weeks at full pay in 2024, meaning Erskine benefited from the new policy when his second child was born 17 months ago. Continue reading...
items.body:
“Being able to take six weeks’ paid paternity leave, flexibly, made a huge difference to me and my family, giving me the time to support my partner and settle into being a new parent,” said Marks & Spencer employee Joe Erskine.
The food and clothing retailer increased its paternity leave offering from two to six weeks at full pay in 2024, meaning Erskine benefited from the new policy when his second child was born 17 months ago.
M&S and Tesco are among the retailers leading the way in offering enhanced paternity leave to their staff, new research has shown, highlighting the widening gap between the more family-friendly policies offered to new fathers working in the retail sector compared with those in construction, manufacturing and agriculture.
Both companies offer six weeks at full pay to employees, far outstripping the statutory two-week minimum paternity leave offer and making them among the most generous of UK blue-chip companies listed on the FTSE 100, according to figures compiled by campaign group The Dad Shift and Ian Dinwiddy of Inspiring Dads.
Privately owned companies Ikea, Lego and Virgin Media O2 now also offer more weeks of fully paid leave to new fathers.
The enhanced paternity leave offered by retailers including Asda, Waitrose and Lidl in recent years means that just five employers are responsible for upgrading parental leave for nearly 650,000 workers.
Retail businesses and the shop workers’ union Usdaw held a roundtable discussion in parliament, hosted by Labour MP Connor Rand, to discuss the transformation in working parents’ lives brought in by changes to parental leave.
Rand, who was a researcher for Usdaw prior to his election to parliament in 2024, said the entitlement was crucial for his family: “Through the ups and downs, I could bond with my son and support my partner because of paternity leave. Too many dads in our country can’t do this. That’s bad for them, bad for their partner and bad for their children. It must change.”
Campaigners have long argued that the UK has one of the least generous paternity leave offers in the world, ranked 40th out of 43 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries. Over two decades after paternity leave rights were introduced in Britain, they argue the country has fallen behind and now has the least generous entitlement in Europe.
Employed fathers in the UK are entitled to two weeks’ statutory paternity leave paid at £194.32 a week, or 90% of their average weekly earnings, whichever amount is lower, totalling less than half the national living wage.
Many companies offer enhanced paternity leave by topping up the statutory offer to full salary, in some cases for a longer period of time.
However, there is a growing disparity between different sectors of the economy. Analysis by The Dad Shift found that the construction sector employs around one in 10 working men, but only accounts for about one in 15 recipients of statutory paternity pay.
This could partly be because some construction workers are self-employed and currently have no entitlement to paid paternity leave, as is also the case for many of Britain’s agricultural workers, the majority of whom are self-employed.
Construction company JCB only offers two weeks’ full pay in paternity leave, although this has been increased from the three days it previously offered.
Engineering firm Rolls-Royce, which makes jet engines for planes, turbines for ships and small nuclear power plants, has a workforce that is more than 80% male but currently only offers two weeks’ fully paid leave.
More than 100 Labour MPs have called on Andy Burnham in recent weeks to commit to improving the UK’s paternity leave in the upcoming budget, warning that lowest-paid fathers are the hardest hit by inadequate paternity leave provision.
They are calling for the introduction of six weeks of paternity leave paid at 90% of earnings, capped at £1,200 a week, with the offer extended to self-employed fathers. An 18-month government review of the UK’s parental leave system is expected to report later this year.

items.body:
Oak Furnitureland will open a new showroom at Riverside Retail Park in Northampton today bringing its collection of stylish, high-quality furniture to more customers across Northamptonshire.
The 12,500sq ft showroom will showcase the retailer’s expanding ‘Whole Home’ proposition, featuring fully styled room sets to help customers visualise looks across living, dining, bedroom and home office spaces.
To celebrate the opening, the first 100 visitors will receive a complimentary goodie bag filled with treats to take home and enjoy.
Northampton shoppers can also be among the first to try the new Santorini sofa range, launching this weekend. Available in multiple sizes, across 8 leather colours 4 neutral fabrics, it features an extending motion chaise, offering extra room to stretch out, and a telescopic headrest that adjusts for added comfort.
Customers can also try the new Cassius CineLuxe sofa, complete with built-in speakers, a console panel, heated and vibrating seats, and cup coolers for a cinema experience at home – perfect for film fans.
Alongside sofas, Oak Furnitureland’s key cabinetry ranges will also be on display, including the Noah solid mango wood dining tables, sideboards and TV units, plus the Scandi-inspired Oaklee dining set and sideboard, with bevelled edges and a rich walnut finish.
The opening has created seven new jobs locally, including roles across sales, showroom management and customer support.
Ruth Johnson, store manager at the new Northampton showroom, said: “There’s nothing quite like trying new potential furniture for yourself- whether that’s a new sofa for family movie nights, or choosing the perfect dining table for a full house at Christmas. We’re excited to open our doors and help shoppers in Northampton to do just that this week.
“We’ve got a brilliant opening weekend planned, with goodie bags for our first 100 visitors and the chance to try out our brand-new Santorini sofa range. Our new team can’t wait to meet everyone and help them find pieces they’ll love for years to come.”
Alex Fisher, chief executive of Oak Furnitureland, said: “It’s exciting to welcome Northampton to our network of 70 showrooms across the UK, creating seven local jobs and bringing our furniture to even more customers. The new showroom brings our Whole Home offering to life, helping customers find inspiration and choose stylish, properly made furniture at outstanding prices. We can’t wait to open the doors and welcome customers from across Northamptonshire.”
Last year, the retailer launched its Lifetime Furniture Guarantee which covers the structural framework of both cabinet and upholstery collections – demonstrating the brand’s commitment to furniture which is built to last. It also offers interest-free credit options to help customers create their ideal home at affordable prices.
With 70 showrooms nationwide, Oak Furnitureland continues to invest in its retail estate, enhancing the in-store experience for our customers.

The award, sponsored by Space Solutions, […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Green Fulfilment has won Best Use of Digital Technology at the 28th Glasgow Business Awards. The award recognises the Go Green platform and the wider set of tools the company’s in-house development team has built to run eCommerce fulfilment for more than 100 brands across the UK and Europe.
The award, sponsored by Space Solutions, was presented on Thursday night at a black-tie ceremony hosted by Glasgow Chamber of Commerce at the DoubleTree by Hilton Glasgow Central. Green Fulfilment was one of six finalists in a category that recognises businesses that have built digital technology into their operations to improve efficiency, growth and the customer experience.
Technology clients can feel
Green Fulfilment launched its Go Green platform in 2022. For the brands it works with, that means one place to see their stock, orders, deliveries and returns, wherever they sell online, from their own website to Amazon and TikTok Shop. Orders flow straight from a brand’s online shop to the warehouse floor, so nothing is typed in twice and parcels go out quicker and more accurately.
Because the developers sit alongside the warehouse teams, the platform keeps improving in the ways clients actually ask for. This year that has meant:
- Greener choices: showing brands the carbon footprint of their deliveries, so they can report on it and act on it
- Personalised products made simple: from embroidered names to engraved gifts, orders are personalised just in time.
- Clearer returns: brands can follow every return and see how quickly it was processed
- Problems spotted early: a delayed order or stock issue is flagged to the team before the customer notices
- Faster answers: routine “where is my order?” questions are answered quicker
- Less paperwork: HR, training and day-to-day procedures now run through the company’s own systems, freeing staff to focus on customers’ orders
Cain Fleming, co-founder and chief technical director of Green Fulfilment, said: “We decided early on to have our own developers and build around how our warehouses actually work. When a client needs something done differently, our team can change it instead of waiting on someone else’s roadmap. That’s how we’ve added personalisation, carbon reporting and a new returns portal in a single year. This award belongs to the developers and the warehouse teams who build and test it together every day, and winning it in our home city makes it even better.”
Rukhsar Ahmed, co-founder and managing director, added: “Clients come to us to get orders out the door, not for software. What the tech team has built means they can see exactly what’s happening with their stock, and our warehouse teams spend less time on paperwork and more time on fulfilment. I’m really proud of everyone involved.”
A third year of recognition in Glasgow
This is the third year in a row Green Fulfilment and its founders have been recognised at the Glasgow Business Awards. Cain Fleming won Young Business Person of the Year in 2024, and the company won the Green Champion Award, sponsored by ScottishPower, in 2025. Cain was also a finalist for Entrepreneur of the Year at this year’s awards.
The win caps a strong week for the company. On Sunday 27 September, Green Fulfilment was named Business of the Year at the Scottish Muslim Awards, with co-founder Rukhsar Ahmed accepting the award.
Founded in Glasgow in 2016 by Rukhsar Ahmed and Cain Fleming, Green Fulfilment became a certified B Corp in 2024 and opened its European fulfilment hub in Venlo, Netherlands, in 2025.

items.title: Fraudsters expected to pounce on bad weather and offer urgent home 'repairs', warns major bank
items.summary: Homeowners are at risk of being swindled by fraudsters pouncing on upcoming storms and bad weather, a major high street bank warns.
items.body:
Fraudsters expected to pounce on bad weather and offer urgent home 'repairs', warns major bank
Homeowners are at risk of being swindled by fraudsters pouncing on storms and bad weather, a major high street bank warns.
Crooks are expected to use the heavy rain forecast this winter to urge homeowners to pay for urgent repairs to their property, Santander says.
Unscrupulous tricksters could turn up on doorsteps, claiming repairs are needed following storms or changes need to be made to your home to prepare for future severe rain or wind.
Families are battening down the hatches to weather Storm Austen and then Boelo.
And almost two in five homeowners believe their home will be vulnerable to flooding in the next five years.
The stormy conditions combined with this worry could create a perfect recipe of urgency and stress to make households more susceptible to a crook's wily tricks.
Storm scammers: Tricksters to take advantage of bad weather this winter
Chris Ainsley, of Santander, says: 'With heavy rain and flooding on the cards this winter, many homeowners could be facing urgent repairs to make sure their homes and families are safe.
'Unfortunately, scammers know that people under pressure have less time to think and make those checks they normally would.
'If a trader knocks at your door or gives you a ring unexpectedly, either claiming work must be done immediately, or asking for a large payment upfront, stop and ask yourself if it feels right.'
Scammers conned some £5.37million out of unsuspecting households in building related scams – including advance fee, purchase and impersonation scams – between January and September, the bank says.
In March, some £1million was handed over the scammers for fake or questionable building work after one of the wettest winters on record.
Crooks made contact via Facebook, cold calling or even a friends recommendations.
What to do if your house needs work
If someone tells you unprompted that your house needs repairing or storm proofing, don't feel rushed to do anything about it.
A legitimate tradesman wouldn't rush you or say you need to act immediately.
Instead, get an expert opinion from a trader you have found independently. Check reviews and credentials.
If you do need work to repair damages caused by a storm or ahead of future storms, get multiple quotes.
Ask for them in writing and make sure the agreed work, total cost, materials and payment schedule are set out before the work starts, Santander says.
If you're asked for a substantial deposit or there's a sudden change in price, make sure you understand why and don't send any money until you have a clear answer.

items.title: Small shops pushed to stock new products to prop up sales as costs mount ahead of the Budget
items.summary: Small retailers are banking on new products to boost sales as rising costs and weaker consumer spending pile pressure on firms ahead of the Budget.
items.body:
Small shops pushed to stock new products to prop up sales as costs mount ahead of the Budget
Small retailers are banking on new products to boost sales as rising costs and weaker consumer spending pile pressure on firms ahead of the Budget.
Almost half of small retailers increased revenue over the past 12 months despite a difficult trading environment, while 96 per cent said diversifying their businesses was essential to future success, according to research by Zempler Bank.
The high street has been hit by a toxic mix of rising costs, taxes and dampened consumer appetite, driven in part by the Middle East conflict, which has sent energy prices higher.
Despite the conditions, independent retailers have proved resilient, with 48 per cent reporting higher revenue over the past year, while only 5 per cent reported a decline.
The figures suggest that while the sector continues to eke out growth, retailers and other small firms are doing so against a backdrop of subdued demand.
Small and micro businesses, employing up to ten people, cite lower consumer spending as the most significant barrier to growth.
Independent retailers are battling mounting costs and fewer customers
Sunder Sandher, who runs a OneStop convenience store in Leamington Spa, said: 'With the cost of living rising, customers are more careful with their spending, while our own business expenses continue to increase.
'I'm adapting by managing costs carefully, stocking what customers need and keeping prices competitive.'
Consumer confidence has slumped to its lowest level in more than three years, driven by cost-of-living pressures and fears of interest rate hikes.
At the same time, high street footfall has proved sluggish, falling 3 per cent in September.
Half of those surveyed pointed to rising operating costs, while 30 per cent highlighted higher staffing costs, with almost all (96 per cent) believing diversification is essential to their future.
That has prompted seven in ten retailers to pin their hopes on new stock to drive growth, with 77 per cent planning to launch new product categories in the next 12 months.
It echoes similar moves by food chains, including Greggs and Domino's, that have introduced new ranges to cater to changing tastes.
Smaller hospitality firms are similarly reinventing themselves by launching separate ghost kitchen brands designed exclusively for delivery and hosting pop-ups in pubs.
Dee Sadani says he thinks twice about investing in his businesses
Separate research by Zempler reveals a shift away from major delivery aggregators, such as Deliveroo and Just Eat, as commission costs eat into independents' bottom lines.
Despite efforts to grow, Britain's smallest firms are pleading for change in next week's Budget.
Dee Sadani, who owns three One Stop franchises in Matlock, Stoke and Etwall, says running costs, red tape and 'keep up with all the new rules is very onerous.
Margins are thin, but profit does take a hit because of cost inflation.
He added: 'Theft is a significant problem.
'People steal to sell, so small retailers become a particular target.
'I would love for a politician to spend a day in the life of a retailer to understand the landscape and what we face.
'Small changes mean we can't invest in our business like we did before. We need to think twice.'
Chef Tom Kerridge has called for VAT on hospitality to be cut from 20 per cent to 10 per cent, while Zempler is urging the government to increase the threshold from £90,000 to £150,000.
Alex Rice, chief product and customer officer, said: 'The VAT threshold is a growth question too.
'Too many deliberately hold back turnover to stay under a cliff-edge when lifting it would give them room to grow, take on staff and invest. Be bold and lift it to £150,000.'
He added: 'Whatever their size, our customers want the same thing from this Budget, certainty, not surprises and no own goals on tax that end up raising less while chilling enterprise.'

items.title: More than third of post offices in TG Jones stores to shut by early 2027
items.summary: Closures within chain formerly under the WH Smith brand raise fears of high streets becoming ‘postal deserts’ Towns and even city centres face being left as “postal deserts” after it emerged that more than a third of post offices within the troubled TG Jones chain are closing. So far this year 36 branches within the high street chain formerly known as WH Smith have closed and a further 34 are set to close by early 2027, according to Post Office records analysed by the Guardian. Continue reading...
items.body:
Towns and even city centres face being left as “postal deserts” after it emerged that more than a third of post offices within the troubled TG Jones chain are closing.
So far this year 36 branches within the high street chain formerly known as WH Smith have closed and a further 34 are set to close by early 2027, according to Post Office records analysed by the Guardian.
TG Jones was bought and renamed by Modella last year. Before the private equity group’s restructure won approval from creditors in July, the chain operated 180 post offices and it had been feared that as many as 60 could be closed under the shake-up.
Up to 150 of the 450 stores acquired by Modella are expected to shut, about 65 of which have already closed and at least another 46 are to cease operating early next year. This total of 110 announced closures include the 70 containing post offices.
The larger-than-expected wave of TG Jones branch closures follows an announcement in the summer that 52 post offices will close within Morrisons Daily convenience stores this year, some of which are close to the TG Jones sites. The move forms part of a wider plan by Morrisons to close 100 loss-making small stores.
The raft of closures means that towns such as Stevenage in Hertfordshire, Bracknell in Berkshire and Orpington in Greater London, and some smaller cities including Hull and York are each losing two post offices in a matter of months. Telford’s last one is due to close in January.
The majority of these lost sites replaced former crown post offices, the now almost entirely closed network of more than 100 directly operated large branches, which offered a full suite of services such as identity and passport checks, driving licence and banking operations.
Some regions such as Essex, the West Midlands, Wales, Suffolk and Hertfordshire have been particularly hard hit. Six post offices in TG Jones stores in Essex are going, with Clacton-on-Sea and Brentwood shutting in January after the closure of ones in Basildon, Southend-on-Sea, Harlow and East Ham. Five are closing in the West Midlands and four in Wales.
The Post Office is trying to find new operators in these locations but so far only Stirling has reopened after a TG Jones closure, and a permanent replacement for Ipswich is set to open in November. Temporary branches are to operate after TG Jones closures in Maidenhead and Uxbridge.
Such losses can be devastating to the health of local economies. As the Post Office itself pointed out to a parliamentary inquiry into revitalising high streets, almost a third of small- and medium-sized businesses use their local branch at least once a week and more than half use the network at least once a month. Many small businesses report that losing this access would threaten their viability within months.
After the closure of more than 6,800 bank branches across the UK, the Post Office “plays a critical role in protecting this essential service”, according to thetstate-owned company’s evidence to the inquiry. Post office operators already run 250 banking hubs, which combine services for several banking brands, across the UK.
Mole Meade, a senior member at the CWU, the largest union for postal workers, said the closures would leave some areas as “postal deserts”.
Meade added: “What we are seeing with the TG Jones closures is the continuation of a long-term strategy of cutting costs and chasing profit, with little regard for the communities that depend on post office services.
“The CWU believes the Post Office should be focused on protecting and expanding access to services, not presiding over a continued reduction of the network.”
The Post Office said: “We fully recognise the challenging trading conditions that TG Jones and many other high street retailers are facing at the moment. We proactively sought expressions of interest from our postmasters and partners to take on post offices within TG Jones stores that may close as a result of their restructuring plan or any decisions taken by landlords.
“There is interest in taking on every location where it has been confirmed that a post office within a TG Jones store will close. In some locations there are over 40 applications from our postmasters who recognise the significant footfall operating a post office brings to their store … We’re committed to replacing every branch within a TG Jones store that closes and are working to progress applications as quickly as possible.”
The state-owned Post Office – which is still reeling from the Horizon IT scandal – announced the closure of more than 100 branches in late 2024.
WH Smith travel stores in railway stations, hospitals and airports were not part of the Modella deal and remain owned by its original stock market-listed parent company.
TG Jones was approached for comment.

M&S Food is making high-quality British meat even better value for customers, with a new investment to make selected family favourite British beef, lamb and pork products more affordable. The investment will see prices of Diced British Beef (500g) fall to £6.00 from £7.00; British Lamb Mince (400g) reduce to £5.60 from £6.20 and British Pork Sausages fall to £2.00 from £2.60.
The investment will make it easier for customers to choose British meat, supporting the farmers who produce it. M&S sources only 100% British beef and lamb and is making this investment while maintaining the long-term partnerships that give farmers confidence to invest in their businesses and plan for the future.
The move forms part of M&S’ wider investment in trusted value, making more shopping list essentials affordable without compromising on quality, sourcing standards or animal welfare. Remarksable Value offers everyday staples benchmarked against competitor prices while maintaining the same market-leading M&S quality customers expect.
At a time when British farmers are facing growing competition from imported meat, M&S continues to strengthen its support for UK agriculture through long-term supplier relationships and its Plan A for Farming strategy. M&S sources 100% British across beef, lamb, chicken, pork and eggs, helping provide confidence and stability for British farming communities while making it easier for customers to choose British.
M&S has long-term strategic agreements in place with key British meat suppliers, including 10-year partnerships with ABP and Dunbia. These partnerships support consistent quality, high animal welfare standards and long-term investment across British farming. For sausages, M&S also has a long-term partnership with Cranswick, further reinforcing its commitment to British agriculture.
Alex Freudmann, managing director of M&S Food, said: “British farmers play a vital role in producing the high-quality food our customers expect, and we’re committed to backing them for the long term. That’s why we’re investing to make our British beef, lamb and pork more affordable for customers while continuing to support farmers through the long-term partnerships that provide confidence to invest in their businesses. At a time when British farmers are facing increasing pressure, we’re proud to champion British produce, support high standards of welfare and quality, and help more customers choose British meat at M&S.”
John Egerton, M&S Select Beef farmer, said: “As farmers, we need confidence to invest in our businesses for the long term. M&S’s commitment to British farming, backed by long-term partnerships and investment, helps provide that certainty. At a time when British farmers are facing increasing competition from imported products, it’s great to see more customers being encouraged to choose high-quality British meat while knowing the farmers behind it continue to be supported.”
The investment forms part of M&S’ wider strategy to make it easier for customers to do more of their weekly shop at M&S, combining trusted value with the quality, sourcing standards and animal welfare standards customers expect.

items.body:
The female-founded British fashion brand continues to expand its UK retail presence, bringing its latest Paris-shot Party Collection to Manchester and Birmingham.
British fashion brand Never Fully Dressed announces its return to Selfridges this October, launching three dedicated pop-ups across Manchester Trafford, Manchester Exchange and Birmingham, marking another exciting moment in the brand’s continued retail expansion.
Founded in East London by Lucy Aylen in 2009, Never Fully Dressed has grown from its Market stall beginnings into an internationally recognised fashion brand, celebrated for its distinctive prints, statement, in-house designs and inclusive approach to dressing. The return to Selfridges further strengthens the brand’s UK retail presence, bringing its signature feel-good fashion to new audiences across two key regional shopping destinations.
Arriving just in time for the festive season, the pop-ups will showcase Never Fully Dressed’s latest Party Collection, a celebration of statement dressing, individuality and the joy of getting dressed. Think sequins, playful feathers, rich textures and versatile multi-wear silhouettes designed to take you from festive celebrations to everyday moments always worth dressing up for.
Shot in Paris and fronted by Grace Ghanem, the latest campaign captures the confidence, creativity and playful spirit at the heart of Never Fully Dressed. Set against the streets of the French capital, the collection brings together statement silhouettes and unexpected styling, celebrating an approach to party dressing that feels expressive, effortless and unapologetically individual.
With a growing international community and an expanding retail footprint, Never Fully Dressed continues to build on its distinctive positioning within the contemporary fashion market. Its commitment to inclusivity, with collections available in UK sizes 6–26, alongside signature in- house designed prints and multi-wear pieces, remains central to the brand’s identity.
The Selfridges partnership offers a further opportunity to connect with customers through a physical retail experience, allowing shoppers to discover, try on and style the collection in person as the brand continues to strengthen its omnichannel presence.
No party like an NFD party.
Discover Never Fully Dressed at Selfridges Manchester Trafford, Manchester Exchange and Birmingham this October, online at Selfridges.com and in stores nationwide.

items.body:
Co-op Wholesale and experienced convenience store operator VST have signed a new five-year contract for 35 stores, which it officially marked with a grand opening of the debut store in the partnership – Loop Convenience Weymouth.
The extensive arrangement, which will see VST stores converting to Loop Convenience with Proud To Stock Co-op opening throughout the Southwest and along the South Coast, marks a significant milestone for both businesses, who are seeking ambitious growth in these regions.
The former Spar site – a 2,000sq ft unit based at 216 Preston Road – has undertaken a full internal refit while a new fascia will proudly display the Loop Convenience branding externally alongside Proud to Stock Co-op signage, signalling the presence of Co-op Brand goods in store.
Designed to suit the demands of the community it serves, the proposition has been strategically crafted. Food to Go lines including sandwiches, wraps and salads are on shelf while a Co-op Brand in-store bakery stocking popular classic and seasonal lines such as fresh bread, cookies and pastries will occupy a prominent position. The store will also pride itself on having full shelves of fresh and chilled food, treats and snacks, soft drinks, BWS and much more to meet the needs of its shoppers.
As a Proud to Stock Co-op shop, all VST Loop Convenience stores will benefit from access to the full Co-op Brand portfolio, currently boasting over 2,000 products, and all orderable via Co-op Wholesale’s OCS platform.
Co-op Wholesale’s charity – Making A Difference Locally (MADL) provides a true USP. The charity donates funds to support local charities based directly on in-store spend. As part of the launch, MADL has donated £500 to a local cause chosen by VST, which is Margaret Green Animal Rescue centre.
Ian King, business development and growth director at Co-op Wholesale, said: “Our new partnership with VST is one we’re exceptionally proud of as they’re a highly reputable and well-scaled operator across the south coast and southwest. We’re confident we can support its ambitious growth trajectory through our excellent knowledge of wholesaling and highly skilled and supportive teams. The Weymouth store is looking fantastic, too!”
Vijayananth Jaganathan, director at VST, said: “We’re delighted to have entered into this new contract with Co-op Wholesale. Moving 35 of our VST Loop Convenience stores to the Proud To Stock Co-op proposition feels very timely as we believe customers will enjoy shopping the Co-op Brand in our stores now more than ever thanks to its broad range, excellent quality and strong value. We’re grateful for the support of the Co-op Wholesale colleagues who have extremely supportive throughout.”

B&M, the UK’s leading variety retailer, will open its new store at Thistles Shopping Centre in Stirling on Saturday 28 November, creating 15 new jobs and bringing more choice for shoppers ahead of Christmas.
Occupying a 13,012 sq ft space within the former Debenhams unit, the new store marks a major milestone in the ongoing transformation of one of the centre’s most prominent retail spaces.
The store will offer an extensive range of great value homeware, food, health and beauty and seasonal products, alongside DIY essentials, toys, games and gifts, all at the competitive prices for which the brand is known.
David McColl, area manager at B&M, said: “We’re really excited to be opening our new B&M store in Stirling on 28th November. The team is working hard to get everything ready, and we can’t wait to welcome the local community through the doors and show them what the new store has to offer.”
Gary Turnbull, centre director at Thistles, said: “We’re delighted B&M will be opening its door at Thistles ahead of Christmas. Bringing a much-loved brand into the former Debenhams unit is a really positive step for the centre and reflects the continued demand we’re seeing from both retailers and shoppers.
“We’re looking forward to welcoming B&M to the centre and seeing visitors enjoy everything the new store has to offer.”
B&M’s arrival will bring a prominent part of the former Debenhams unit back into use and give shoppers more choice at Thistles as Christmas shopping gets underway.
For more information visit www.thistlesstirling.com.

items.body:
New Look, one of the UK’s leading fashion brands, is reopening its newly refurbished store at Cribbs Causeway in Bristol today, unveiling an improved shopping environment, dedicated spaces for its latest collections and a weekend of celebrations for customers.
To mark the reopening, New Look will be treating shoppers to special surprises, including goody bags for the first 100 customers who make a purchase, prizes hidden throughout the store and complimentary coffee across the weekend.
The refurbished store will showcase New Look’s latest womenswear, footwear and accessories collections, with an updated layout to make it easier for customers to browse and discover new styles.
For the first time, the store will also feature a dedicated 915 space with its own branded entrance from the shopping centre. Designed to give younger customers a place to explore the latest trends and discover their personal style, the new area offers a more independent shopping experience while remaining connected to the main New Look store.
The refreshed store spans over 9,000 sq ft and includes a returns kiosk, part of a wider rollout across New Look’s store estate designed to make online returns and exchanges quicker and more convenient for customers.
The refurbishment forms part of New Look’s continued investment in its bricks-and-mortar estate and wider omnichannel strategy. It builds on recent openings and upgrades across the UK, including at Lakeside, Milton Keynes and Stoke-on-Trent, as well as the opening of its largest-ever concept store at Metrocentre this summer.
Alongside its store programme, New Look continues to grow its loyalty programme, Club New Look, which has surpassed one million members, while strengthening its digital capabilities through a £30 million investment. Together, these initiatives are helping New Look create a more personalised, seamless and connected shopping experience for customers across its physical and digital channels.
Mark Matthews, chief retail and digital officer at New Look, said: “We’re delighted to reopen our Cribbs Causeway store and welcome customers back to a refreshed space that showcases the best of New Look.
“As we continue to invest in our stores, we’re focused on creating shopping environments that reflect how our customers want to shop. At Cribbs Causeway, that includes introducing our first 915 space with its own entrance, giving younger shoppers a dedicated place to explore fashion and develop their own sense of style.
“We’re proud of the changes we’ve made, and hope customers enjoy discovering everything the refreshed store has to offer.”
Iain Minto, senior director, asset management at Sovereign Centros by CBRE, said: “New Look’s impressive store refit is another example of an established UK retailer investing in its Cribbs space as we become a hub for brands to test new concepts and product ranges.
“New Look’s store will act as a showroom with shoppers of all ages from across the West Country, West Midlands, South West, and South Wales travelling to explore their latest styles and trends.”

items.title: Top court rejects Tesco appeal in ‘equal pay’ case
items.summary: The Supreme Court has blocked Tesco from appealing a key ruling in a long-running equal pay claim brought by more than 16,000 shop workers. Tesco is one of several UK supermarkets caught in a legal battle over allegations that it underpays its store workers, mainly women, compared with distribution centre workers, who are mostly men. [...]
items.body:
Top court rejects Tesco appeal in ‘equal pay’ case
The Supreme Court has blocked Tesco from appealing a key ruling in a long-running equal pay claim brought by more than 16,000 shop workers.
Tesco is one of several UK supermarkets caught in a legal battle over allegations that it underpays its store workers, mainly women, compared with distribution centre workers, who are mostly men.
The case, launched in 2018 by claimant-focused law firms Harcus Parker and Leigh Day, now involves thousands of retail employees in separate cases against Asda, Next, Sainsbury’s, Morrisons, and the Co-Op. It is reportedly worth a potential £4bn.
In the case against Tesco, the claims were divided into three stages, but the back-and-forth stems from the Employment Tribunal deciding to use generic training documents, rather than individual daily duties, to define ‘work’ at the hearings.
Tesco appealed through multiple courts to stop the Tribunal from using this definition. Both the Employment Appeal Tribunal and the Court of Appeal partially allowed Tesco’s appeals, but both rejected its main argument that the Tribunal’s overall methodology should be overturned.
The retail giant sought to appeal to the Supreme Court, but the UK’s top court rejected the case earlier this month and refused its application.
As a result, the case will proceed to trial under the Employment Tribunals’ established methodology for defining ‘work’.
Kiran Daurka, employment partner at Leigh Day, said: “This is a significant outcome for the 16,000 Tesco workers we represent and brings Tesco’s challenge on this issue to an end.” He added, “We remain focused on securing equal pay for our clients in the wider litigation.”
A Tesco spokesperson said: “The jobs in our stores and distribution centres are different. These roles require different skills and demands which lead to variations in pay, but this has absolutely nothing to do with gender.
“We are committed to rewarding our colleagues fairly for the jobs they do and work collaboratively with our colleagues and unions to ensure the pay and benefits we offer are fair, competitive and sustainable. Our position in relation to these claims remains unchanged and we continue to strongly defend them,” they added.
Next’s recent dodge in its equal pay case
Last month, retail giant Next won an appeal in its equal pay case, allowing it to pay warehouse workers more than shop-floor staff, and warned that its defeat “would have represented a hammer blow to retail employment in the UK”.
This follows a 2024 Employment Tribunal ruling that the FTSE giant failed to show that paying its sales consultants, most of whom are women, lower hourly rates than staff in its male-dominated warehouses was not sex discrimination.
The retailer was on the line for a £30m payout before it appealed.
But the Employment Appeal Tribunal overturned the landmark decision, citing recruitment and retention pressures that do not apply to sales workers.

items.title: The Weekly Closeout: Torrid CFO exits and Belk secures financing
items.summary: Paula Dempsey will leave the apparel retailer next month. The department store, meanwhile, will use some of its new funds for seasonal inventory.
items.body:
It’s been another week with far more retail news than there is time in the day. Below, we break down some things you may have missed during the week, and what we’re still thinking about.
From the world’s largest cowboy hat to rising childcare costs, here’s our closeout for the week.
What you may have missed
Torrid’s CFO departs
Torrid Chief Financial Officer Paula Dempsey will exit to pursue a new opportunity, the apparel retailer announced Monday. She worked at the retailer for just under four years after leaving Mattress Firm, per LinkedIn.
While Dempsey will remain in the role through mid-November to support a transition, Torrid has named Will Langley as interim CFO, effective Wednesday. Langley comes from Belk where he worked for about 20 years until 2025.
“I am excited to welcome Will to Torrid,” CEO Lisa Harper said in a statement. “He is a seasoned finance leader whose breadth of experience and strategic contributions at Belk make him well suited to guide our finance organization. Having worked with Will for many years, I look forward to the perspective he will bring to Torrid as we continue to execute on our priorities.”
Harper served as CEO of Belk from 2016 until 2021.
Cooper Flagg makes himself at home at Foot Locker
The latest iteration of Foot Locker’s “Hoops Lives Here” campaign went live this week, starring NBA player Cooper Flagg. In the spot, Flagg helps out Foot Locker store associates by stocking the store with the latest releases from his brand sponsor, New Balance.
It’s part of a broader strategy by Foot Locker to invest in basketball. In addition to the campaign, Foot Locker recently became the athletic footwear retailer for the New York Knicks and this week celebrated the team’s championship win with exclusive footwear and apparel at its 33rd Street store in New York City.
"Foot Locker has always been the home for basketball, connecting fans to the athletes, products and culture that define the game," Foot Locker Chief Marketing Officer Brett O'Brien said in a statement. "As we tip off a new NBA season, we're proud to partner with New Balance on this new chapter of 'Hoops Lives Here,' bringing fans closer to the game through product, storytelling and experiences."
Retail therapy
Everything really is bigger in Texas
Western boot brand Tecovas and Circuit of The Americas have teamed up to introduce the world’s largest cowboy hat at The Circuit. And they’ve got the Guinness World Records certification to prove it.
The hat is a recreation of Tecovas’ Cattleman Cowboy Hat, and its debut comes ahead of the Formula 1 United States Grand Prix.
While the sheer size of the hat is remarkable — 43 feet wide by 47 feet long by 17 feet tall, not including piers — what’s arguably most impressive is that the structure features a fully-operational bar under the hat where patrons can enjoy a drink.
"The World's Largest Cowboy Hat belongs in Texas, and there's no better place to welcome fans from around the world with a statement this big," Bobby Epstein, chairman of Circuit of The Americas, said in a statement. "This is a beautiful piece of art with a practical purpose- a place for fans to gather, enjoy some shade, and experience a little Texas hospitality.”
What we’re still thinking about
$1.275B
That’s how much Belk secured in new financing from Wells Fargo and Pathlight Capital. The financing is a $900 million asset-based revolving credit facility and a $375 million first in, last out term loan, according to a Tuesday press release from Pathlight Capital.
The five-year financing replaces Belk’s current ABL, FILO and securitization facilities. The department store will use it to finance its capital needs, seasonal inventory and other corporate purposes.
"This opportunistic financing represents an important milestone and reflects the continued strength in Belk's business by providing us with the flexibility to continue investing in our business and serving our customers," Belk CFO Vince Phelan said in a statement.
What we’re watching
Spiking child care costs add to U.S. consumers’ financial burden, rising more than rent or medical care
Consumers, especially those in lower-income households, are under immense financial pressure heading into the holidays. Affordability has become a watchword in mid-term election campaigns, and concerns about prices and the job market recently sent consumer sentiment to multi-year lows.
Bank of America economic experts recently found that the cost of child care is adding to those woes. The share of U.S. households whose monthly child care costs top $2,000 has more than doubled in the last three years, as those paying $1,000 or less has declined, according to research this week from the Bank of America Institute. Last month, child care and school fees rose more than expenses like rent and medical services, according to the report, citing the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The situation is affecting middle-aged generations most. More than half of households paying for child care were older millennials, followed by younger millennials (20%) and Gen X (16%), Bank of America found. Over the past three months, the growth in older millennial households earning more than one paycheck has abated, suggesting that child care costs could be influencing their decisions about work — something that affects women in particular, the researchers found.

items.title: Supermarkets blindsided by ‘shambolic’ stockpiling warning
items.summary: Supermarkets have been caught off guard by the government’s “shambolic” campaign to urge Brits to stock up on supplies of food and water, industry sources told City AM.  Retailers were not told the details of the government’s “Be Ready” campaign until days before it was announced and expected it to be a more “low key” [...]
items.body:
Supermarkets blindsided by ‘shambolic’ stockpiling warning
Supermarkets have been caught off guard by the government’s “shambolic” campaign to urge Brits to stock up on supplies of food and water, industry sources told City AM.
Retailers were not told the details of the government’s “Be Ready” campaign until days before it was announced and expected it to be a more “low key” affair, the people said.
On Thursday, defence secretary Wes Streeting urged Brits to prepare three days’ worth of non-perishable food and bottled water, an FM radio and blankets in case of hybrid attacks by “hostile state actors or terrorists”.
The defence secretary’s intervention headlined a three-year campaign designed to prepare Brits for the risks posed by technological dependency, hostile state threats and the impact of extreme weather on global supply chains.
Government officials briefed retailers on the date of this announcement only last week, the people said, telling bosses the campaign would be “low key” and fronted by security minister Dan Jarvis.
One senior industry figure said they were surprised to see Streeting leading the news of the new campaign. “It became a big deal because it’s Wes,” they said.
Though retailers were caught off guard by Streeting’s involvement, the defence secretary was not directly involved in the campaign’s launch and made his comments in response to media questions on the topic.
The government’s attempts to ensure that retailers and suppliers could keep up with increased demand for products like bottled water were “shambolic,” a retail industry source said.
During early discussions about the campaign last month, government officials said they had only spoken to Thames Water to ensure that supplies of water could meet demand, City AM understands.
Retailers then told officials that they should speak to bottled water suppliers, not utility firms, about their ability to provide the necessary stock. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs is regularly in contact with the water industry, it is understood.
One major supermarket is holding talks with its suppliers to work out whether the campaign will cause a rush in demand for essentials.
The grocer stressed that Brits have been told to gradually build up their supplies of essentials rather than immediately assemble significant stockpiles.
A corporate affairs official at another top supermarket said this “wouldn’t be the first time” the defence secretary has “overcommunicated”. Grocers are confident they can meet demand for essentials, it is understood.
Food shortage fears
During the Covid-19 pandemic, a rush of panic-buying forced supermarkets like Aldi, Tesco and Waitrose to impose temporary caps on the sale of some products to prevent shortages.
Ged Futter, a former Asda buyer who now advises suppliers on how to negotiate with retailers, said the government’s new campaign is “done with the right intentions, but what you never know is how everybody will interpret it.
“Some will take it seriously and think: ‘Whatever the government says, that’s not going to be enough so I’m going to go for more’. Others will completely ignore it, and that’s the difficulty that a retailer has.”
The British Retail Consortium, which represents top supermarkets including Tesco, Sainsbury’s and Asda, has been in talks with the government about the new campaign.
Jim Bligh, the trade body’s director of food policy, said: “It is sensible for households to be prepared for extreme events, particularly given that people in the UK are less prepared for emergencies than their European neighbours.
“This advice brings the UK more in line with other countries and encourages people to build up a small supply of essentials gradually by simply adding an extra tin or other long-life item to their usual shop from time to time.”
Security minister Dan Jarvis said: “This is just the sort of community-focused campaign the UK needs to improve our resilience as a nation. It will bring us into line with European counterparts, where advice like this is a normal part of everyday life.”

items.title: Bestway aims to give more help to independent retailers
items.summary: Bestway Wholesale has strengthened its field sales operation for independent retailers by appointing 23 dedicated territory sales managers. The new managers are intended to help independent retailers increase sales and profit, with a structure designed to support independent operators with more face-to-face engagement and practical… This story continues at Bestway aims to give more help to independent retailers Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The new managers are intended to help independent retailers increase sales and profit, with a structure designed to support independent operators with more face-to-face engagement and practical advice.
The 23 area managers will be supported by two field sales managers covering the North and South, reporting to a national retail controller.
The idea is that the new managers will work closely with retailers to understand their individual needs.
Support will include reviewing product ranges and category performance, identifying gaps, and improving promotions.
Dan Lewis, sales director for Bestway Wholesale and Bestway Retail, said: “Independent retailers are at the heart of our business, and we recognise the important role we play in helping them remain competitive and profitable.
“Our ambition is simple: to help our customers sell more, make more and save more. That means going beyond supplying great products at competitive prices and ensuring retailers have access to the right advice, insight and support to grow their businesses.”
Bestway said one of the reasons it has made the change is that it recognises that retailers face rising costs, changing consumer habits and increased competition.
Naser Khan, managing director at Bestway Wholesale, said: “Independent retailers are the backbone of communities across the UK, and their success is fundamental to our own.
“We know the challenges they face and we are committed to investing in the people, services and capabilities that will help them compete and grow.
“Strengthening our field sales operation is an important part of our wider growth strategy and demonstrates our continued commitment to independent retail.
“We want every customer to see Bestway as a trusted business partner, one that understands their needs, delivers value and actively supports their long-term success.”

items.title: Debenhams boss calls on Labour to slash business costs and help customers
items.summary: Retailers say the loophole is killing the UK High Street as it means foreign companies can undercut British firms, which have been hit with higher employment and business rates in recent years.
items.body:
Debenhams boss calls on Labour to slash business costs and help customers
The boss of Debenhams has called on Labour to slash business costs and close a tax loophole that benefits rival Shein.
Dan Finley, who leads the online retailer which changed its name from Boohoo last year, has become the latest retail chief to make a pre-Budget plea for Labour to help businesses boost growth.
He urged the Government against ‘looking to increase the cost of doing business for businesses in the UK’, as well as anything that would heap pressure on UK consumers.
His plea follows a similar call from the boss of Sainsbury's yesterday. Simon Roberts said the Government must not 'repeat' the last two Budgets, which saw higher costs of employment heaped onto businesses.
Debenhams, where Sex and the City star Kim Cattrall fronts a fashion campaign, has become the latest business to make a plea to the Chancellor ahead of the Budget.
In particular, he wants the Government to speed up closing a customs duty loophole that means overseas rivals can dodge paying tax on low-value parcels to the UK.
Retailers say this policy is killing the UK High Street as it means foreign companies can undercut British firms, which have been hit with higher employment and business rates in recent years.
The Government has said it will move to scrap a rule that allows Shein and Temu to post parcels worth up to £135 to the UK without paying duty before October 2028.
This has been moved from a later deadline of March 2029, but retailers are still furious over the inaction, especially after crackdowns by the European Union and the US.
Finley said: ‘I'd love an acceleration in the low value import threshold reduction and getting that done way before 2029. The US did it in six months. The E.U. did it in 12 months. Why can't we do it in 18 months?’
Finley has pledged to use the Debenhams brand, where Sex and the City star Kim Cattrall fronts a fashion campaign, as a ‘blueprint’ to transform the ailing fortunes of the wider group, whose brands include Gen Z-focused online retailers Boohoo and PrettyLittleThing.
Shares rose 3 per cent on Friday morning after the group pointed to signs of green shoots of recovery, including a return to profit on a profit-before-tax basis for the first time in five years.
Despite gloom over consumer confidence, Finley said he was confident about the golden quarter as the British shopper ‘always comes out for Christmas.’
He said the retailers’ brands are set to cash in on demand for party clothes, and that he expects ‘the little black dress’ to continue to be ‘our number one bestseller’.
The group has been moving away from holding large amounts of its own stock and towards a marketplace model, where third-party brands sell through its platforms in exchange for a fee.
It has also been clamping down on high return rates for brands including Pretty Little Thing and Boohoo.
It recently sold its Sheffield warehouse to rival Primark for £90million, as well as selling its youth fashion brand Nasty Gal US company WSG Brands for £12million.
Profits were £28.3million for the six months to the end of August, swinging from a loss of £17.9million over the same period last year.
Fast-fashion firm Boohoo bought department store chain Debenhams out of administration in 2021, dispensing with its shops in a major blow to the High Street and switching online.
