items.summary: Local shops have welcomed the government's acceptance of recommendations from the Small Business Taskforce to cut red tape and save money in administrative costs. The Small Business Taskforce, which includes the Association of Convenience Stores (ACS), the Federation of Small Businesses, Small Business Britain and… This story continues at Local shops welcome government red tape pledge Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The Small Business Taskforce, which includes the Association of Convenience Stores (ACS), the Federation of Small Businesses, Small Business Britain and others, has been working through the summer to put together 15 recommendations that would make running a business more straightforward and less burdensome, especially when reporting into government.
Key recommendations in the report include:
- Digitisation and standardisation of licensing applications: government should work towards standardising licence applications for alcohol, entertainment, temporary events notices, late-night refreshment and taxis administered by local authorities in England so that businesses only need to provide information once, and introduce guaranteed decision timelines where feasible.
- HMRC should commit to cutting the burden on small businesses when providing the Valuation Office information regarding business rates: information requests can place a significant burden on small businesses, particularly where the information being requested is unnecessary or duplicates information already held by a public body. Therefore, as part of the valuation process, the Valuation Office should, by default, provide pre-populated forms containing all information currently held for a given property.
- Support for small and medium-sized businesses in complying with Natasha’s Law: while the consumer protection objectives of Natasha’s Law are strongly supported, small food businesses can face disproportionately high compliance costs compared with larger operators. Government should convene a working group to agree practical solutions that make it easier for small food and drink businesses to comply with Natasha’s Law, including the feasibility of a free, customisable FSA labelling template.
ACS chief executive Ed Woodall said: “Over two thirds of the UK’s 50,000-plus convenience stores are run by small business owners, working long hours to serve their communities.
“We are pleased that the government has accepted the recommendations put forward in the taskforce’s report, which will together make a positive difference to retailers who will be able to spend more time serving customers and less time doing paperwork.
“Convenience store retailers are especially keen for the government to make progress on the standardisation and modernisation of licence applications.
“This change alone would save a huge amount of time and future-proof the system for the implementation of additional licensing regimes in the coming years.”
Prime minister Andy Burnham said: “If you run a business, you want to spend your time serving your customers, creating jobs and growing your firm, not filling in unnecessary forms.
“It’s not right that pointless bureaucracy gets in the way of people working hard to build something that matters to their high street.”
Chancellor John Healey said: “British firms are fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork that eats into valuable time and money when they simply want to get on with running their businesses.
“That is why we are cutting unnecessary bureaucracy and giving businesses the breathing space they need to invest, innovate and create good jobs.”

items.title: Why investors are betting on sulfur to power the next generation of defence kit
items.summary: The cathode is the part of a battery that stores charge, and today's versions rely on critical minerals that are costly to mine and tricky to source.
items.body:
Why investors are betting on sulfur to power the next generation of defence kit
Imagine a battery that swaps scarce metals for sulfur, one of the cheapest and most plentiful materials on earth.
That is the pitch from Gelion, the London-listed battery technology company, whose cathode material could suit drones, defence kit and aerospace.
The cathode is the part of a battery that stores charge, and today's versions rely on critical minerals that are costly to mine and tricky to source.
Gelion's sulfur alternative is designed to slot into existing factories, which would spare manufacturers from rebuilding their production lines.
Sulfur batteries could prompt a battery breakthrough for military drones and other defence firms
Investors piled in this week, pushing the shares up 55 per cent, after the National Laboratory of the Rockies, a US Department of Energy research centre, reproduced Gelion's results. The lab built its own cells from Gelion's material, and they held 92 per cent of their capacity when the charging speed was raised 20-fold.
Gelion plans to sell the material to other battery makers, who will want proof it works outside the company's own labs. The tests used coin cells, the smallest format, so larger prototypes are the next hurdle.
A brutal week for growth
Turning to the wider market, it has been a fairly brutal week for growth stocks, with the AIM All-Share down 3 per cent as the tech sell-off in the US and global political uncertainty triggered a retreat from the riskier end of the market. Its benchmark, the FTSE 100, fell 2 per cent.
Sticking with the week's winners, a presentation and interview with an industry expert appeared to put the wind in the sails of Pulsar Helium, which jumped 29 per cent.
Ixico, the brain imaging specialist, advanced 26 per cent after it raised revenue expectations. The icing on the cake came a couple of days later when it landed a £1.5million contract to supply its expertise to an Alzheimer's trial.
Landmark for Metals One
It has been a landmark week for Metals One. It signed a term sheet to acquire full ownership of Lions Bay Resources, bringing under its control the Barbrook Gold Mine in South Africa's Mpumalanga Province and the KC Energy Cogeneration Power Plant in Newcastle, KwaZulu-Natal.
CREST Corporate Services has come up with a sum-of-the-parts valuation that suggests the enlarged group is worth just shy of £107million, or 6.1p a share. The stock, up 20 per cent this week, is changing hands for 1.46p.
Big raises, bigger ambitions
The week's list of fallers was headed by two companies raising comparatively significant sums from the junior market.
The idea is that companies discount their shares to bring in new investment, so mechanically this leads to a drop in the price. But the net impact over the longer term is that the capital is put to use creating significant value.
For Cornish Metals, down 26 per cent, the money, some £135million, will be going directly into the ground to develop the South Crofty tin project. As eye-catching as the headline figure was, another number jumped out: the £11.2million contributed by Glencore, the FTSE 100 miner and metal trader. It is one of a host of big-name backers of the Cornish build-out.
The £35million raised by battery company Invinity Energy Systems suggests its backers have faith in its ability to turn the technology into a viable product, even if the shares ended the week 36 per cent lower.
The fuel of the future, still waiting
Finally, green hydrogen has been the fuel of the future for so long that sceptics could be forgiven for thinking it will stay that way.
The economics have never quite worked. The technology has been too expensive, too inefficient, or both. And the big players in the energy sector have been watching and waiting rather than committing.
Hydrogen Solutions, a London-based company founded by James Busche, thinks it has the answer. Its H2 HotBox is a dual-mode solid oxide device that can produce green hydrogen from water and renewable electricity, then run in reverse to generate clean power from that stored hydrogen.
One box, two jobs, and a claimed efficiency well above anything currently on the market.
Still in its embryonic phase, the company hopes to emulate British hydrogen successes such as ITM Power and Ceres Power, which began on AIM before moving up the food chain. Broker CREST Corporate Broking believes the technology could be worth 366 per cent upside on the current share price.

items.title: Retail sales in Great Britain fall as struggling households cut back
items.summary: Latest negative economic update comes as John Healey prepares to announce budget next week Retail sales in Great Britain fell more steeply than expected last month, the latest negative economic update before the chancellor, John Healey, announces his budget next week. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold fell 0.4% month on month in September, much steeper than economists’ consensus expectations of a 0.1% fall. Continue reading...
items.body:
Retail sales in Great Britain fell more steeply than expected last month, the latest negative economic update before the chancellor, John Healey, announces his budget next week.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold fell 0.4% month on month in September, much steeper than economists’ consensus expectations of a 0.1% fall.
The decrease, which was fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter wear because of an unseasonably warm September, comes as figures show consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate since the Covid pandemic.
While retail sales dropped across almost all sectors of the industry, the volume of motor fuel sold soared 2.2% month on month despite prices at the pump hitting record highs, returning to levels last seen before the start of the conflict in the Middle East.
In value terms, the 6.1% increase in fuel sales was the biggest month-on-month increase since 10.9% was recorded in March, the month immediately after the start of the US-Iran conflict.
Stripping out the increase from fuel, retail sales fell 0.7% in September, much worse than the 0.1% fall forecast by the City.
“October’s sharp fall in consumer confidence and the dip in retail sales volumes in September show that times are getting tougher for households just as the all-important festive period for retailers is just around the corner,” said Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics.
“This supports our view that both real consumer spending and real GDP will grind to a halt in [the final quarter of this year and the first quarter of next]. And this fall in consumer confidence is also the kind of thing that makes the prime minister less likely to call an early election soon.”
Non-store retailing, predominantly online sales, fell 2.2% month on month, the biggest percentage fall across the retail sector.
Textile, clothing and footwear stores recorded a 0.9% fall, household goods retailers were hit by a 0.5% sales slump, while supermarkets dipped 0.4%, partly because of poor sales of clothing ranges due to the weather.
The only sector to record an increase in sales last month – apart from automotive fuel – was department stores, where the volume of goods bought rose 0.2%.
The fall in monthly sales follows a bumper August, with the ONS revising figures up from a 0.5% monthly rise to 0.7%.
This helped fuel a 0.7% increase in sales over the three months to the end of September compared with the previous quarter.
“Retail sales grew in the latest quarter with growth led by motor fuel, which, despite recent price increases at the pump, have now returned to monthly sales levels last seen before the start of the conflict in the Middle East,” said Hannah Finselbach, a senior statistician at the ONS. “Food and drink sales also contributed to growth in the quarter, partly helped by the warm weather and the World Cup, although they fell back slightly in September.”

items.title: Facial recognition firm offers retailers free crime reporting platform
items.summary: Facial recognition specialist Facewatch is offering retailers its latest anti-shoplifting technology for free. Facewatch Live is undergoing live testing and will be free to retailers and the police, the company has announced. The platform is designed to give retailers a much clearer understanding of the… This story continues at Facial recognition firm offers retailers free crime reporting platform Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Facewatch Live is undergoing live testing and will be free to retailers and the police, the company has announced.
The platform is designed to give retailers a much clearer understanding of the crime affecting their businesses and can be deployed as a standalone crime reporting solution or sit alongside Facewatch’s established live facial recognition technology.
Used together, the two systems can help retailers understand offending across their stores and target preventative action where it is most needed. Retailers can also use either service independently.
Nick Fisher, chief executive of Facewatch, said: “Live facial recognition has already proved the value of giving retailers accurate, actionable intelligence the moment an offender enters a store.
“Facewatch Live gives retailers the opportunity to record incidents, see the bigger picture in their own crime data, and build stronger evidence against prolific offenders.
“Retailers can decide which system best suits their needs, but feedback from current retail partners who have helped build the platform is that the two systems together offer a powerful force against retail crime.”
Participating retailers will test how the platform brings incidents, CCTV, images, witness information and other supporting evidence together to build a clearer picture of crime across individual stores and entire estates.
Multiple incidents can be associated with the same offender profile, helping retailers identify repeat and prolific offending that can be difficult to recognise when incidents are viewed separately.
Facewatch Live will be available as a completely standalone service, giving retailers free access to record incidents, manage supporting evidence and analyse their own crime data. It will not be necessary for a retailer to subscribe to Facewatch’s Live Facial Recognition service in order to use Facewatch Live.
Fisher added: “We have taken the decision to make Facewatch Live not just free to police, but also completely free to the retail sector. Retail operators should not have to pay simply to understand what is going on in their own businesses, and the process of reporting crime should not come with a price tag.”
Facewatch was originally founded in 2010 as a digital reporting tool to help businesses provide usable incident reports to police. In 2018, Facewatch shifted its focus to prevention using live facial recognition. Budgens and Sainsbury’s are among the the retail clients of Facewatch.
In September 2026, Facewatch’s live facial recognition system generated 81,988 real-time alerts, its fifth consecutive monthly record. In May, the figure was 55,462.

items.title: Hundreds more shoplifters charged by Essex police this year
items.summary: Essex Police reported this week that the force has secured 4,000 shoplifting charges in the past year, 500 more than the previous 12 months, an increase of 12.5%. Assistant chief constable Glen Pavelin said: “More charges and fewer offences – we’re getting a grip of… This story continues at Hundreds more shoplifters charged by Essex police this year Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Assistant chief constable Glen Pavelin said: “More charges and fewer offences – we’re getting a grip of shoplifting.”
Pavelin highlighted the work of the neigbourhood policing and business crime teams in tackling shop theft.
He said: “Now, due to our hard work, over the last year shoplifting levels have fallen with more than 600 fewer offences, and we’re solving more cases.
“Four thousand charges works out as almost 11 secured every day and highlights the success we’re having at putting suspects in front of the courts.”
One part of the force’s effort in tackling shoplifting has been to get suspects into court as quickly as possible.
Pavelin said: “Where the evidence is strong enough, we’re able to go straight to charge rather than having to arrest an offender and bring them in for an interview where they might just go ‘no comment’.
“And, at court, offenders are also more likely to plead guilty due to the weight of evidence against them.”
The Essex force has also been working to obtain criminal behaviour orders (CBOs) against those convicted, which ban offenders from certain shops or areas.
In Chelmsford, there are currently 20 CBOs in place using a combination of enforcement and intervention to challenge harmful behaviour, designed to support positive change and improve the experience of everyone who lives, works and spends time in the city centre.

items.title: UK consumer confidence falls at fastest rate since Brexit vote as cost of living bites
items.summary: Economic fallout from war in Middle East adds to pressures on consumers and on chancellor before budget Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain. With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living. Continue reading...
items.body:
Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain.
With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living.
Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum.
The index – which has been closely tracked by the government and the Bank of England for early warning signs from the economy since the early 1970s – recorded its largest ever fall, of 25 points, in March 2020 just after the start of the first UK lockdown.
The latest snapshot represents a marked change from the summer, when GfK said a “Burnham bounce”, along with a strong World Cup run by the men’s England football team and sunny weather, lifted the mood of consumers in its long-running monthly survey.
Neil Bellamy, consumer insights director at GfK, said: “Relentless cost-of-living pressures, against an international backdrop of unresolved regional conflicts that are themselves contributing to domestic inflation now at 3.5%, appear to have swept aside the nascent optimism we saw following the appointment of a new UK prime minister this summer.”
It comes as consumers face a fresh squeeze on living standards triggered by the unfolding war in the Middle East. Petrol and diesel prices have surged close to record highs and energy bills have increased in advance of a difficult winter for households already feeling the pinch from years of price increases.
Over the past five years analysis by the Trades Union Congress shows that UK households have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills.
With less than a week before his tax and spending speech to the Commons, the chancellor is under pressure to take action to support households amid warnings that consumer energy bills could reach £2,000 a year from January for the typical household.
Healey has pledged to use his statement to announce “breathing space” measures to ease the pressure. However, he has also warned that the government has limited resources to intervene as the Middle East conflict pushes the UK’s borrowing costs to the highest level in decades.
Official figures released on Wednesday show headline inflation rose by more than expected to 3.5% last month, while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn.
In a double blow for the chancellor, the twin pieces of bad news underscore the fact that consumers are facing a renewed cost of living squeeze, just as Healey is also under increased financial pressure.
According to the latest figures from GfK, consumers became less confident about the strength of their own personal finances, as well as the general outlook for the British economy at large.
The major purchase index fell by 14 points to -22 in October, suggesting that consumers could be bracing to cut back on spending over the winter months to make room in their finances for higher energy bills.
Separate figures from the CBI show investment intentions among manufacturing businesses were subdued as cost pressures remained high in the three months to October.
Manufacturing output is expected to stabilise in the next three months, according to the lobby group’s latest Industrial Trends Survey. However, cost pressures for businesses remained elevated.
Cameron Martin, senior economist at the CBI, said: “If the government wants to meaningfully tackle the cost of living, it must give manufacturers the breathing space to invest and drive the productivity growth needed to sustain rising real wages.
“Next week’s budget must deliver this by cutting business electricity costs, reducing labour costs and reforming business rates to support rather than hinder investment and growth.”
The Treasury has been approached for comment.

items.title: 'Extraordinary collapse' sees consumer confidence suffer biggest slump in a decade
items.summary: Britain has suffered an 'extraordinary collapse' in consumer confidence as Trumpflation wipes away hopes of a 'Burnham bounce'.
items.body:
'Extraordinary collapse' sees consumer confidence suffer biggest slump in a decade
Britain has suffered an ‘extraordinary collapse’ in consumer confidence as Trumpflation wipes away hopes of a ‘Burnham bounce’.
Closely-watched figures from market researchers GfK showed confidence has suffered its sharpest drop for a decade this month in what was described as an ‘alarming’ deterioration.
The fall of 11 points to minus 24 in October was the biggest since July 2016 – excluding the pandemic – according to GfK.
Household gloom has deepened particularly over the outlook for the economy. Consumer appetite to make major purchases – such as washing machines and sofas – also slumped.
It comes as Donald Trump’s Iran war continues to result in high global oil and gas prices which have pushed up the price of fuel and household energy in a phenomenon dubbed ‘Trumpflation’.
There is little sign of relief, with oil benchmark Brent crude yesterday hitting $112.68 a barrel, a five-month high.
GfK's consumer confidence Index fell 11 points to minus 24 in October as households struggle with a rise in the cost of living
And wage growth is slowing, with figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) yesterday showing the average salary in Britain increasing by just 4.5 per cent – the weakest since 2021.
GfK’s figures represent a blow to Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s attempts to lift the mood with promises of cost of living help and optimism about reviving prosperity.
And they come just days before a debut Budget from Chancellor John Healey - as his options for delivering relief to consumers are narrowed by the deteriorating state of the public finances.
Neil Bellamy, consumer insights director at GfK, said: ‘There has been an extraordinary collapse in consumer confidence in October.
‘These are damaging findings given the UK government’s priority of economic growth.
‘Relentless cost-of-living pressures… appear to have swept aside the nascent optimism we saw following the appointment of a new UK prime minister this summer.
‘Headline consumer confidence is now back to the level seen in April, May and June of this year and the summer’s buoyant mood has evaporated. The speed of this deterioration is alarming.’
It comes after figures this week showed inflation surging to 3.5 per cent, an 11-month high, thanks to rising petrol and diesel prices.
Inflation is expect to climb to 4 per cent in the new year, with an energy prices increase in January set to push typical household bills towards £2,000.
That is well above the Bank of England’s 2 per cent target, adding to fears that a widely-expected hike in interest rates next month will be followed by further increases over the course of 2027.
Another grim update this week revealed that UK job vacancies have fallen below 700,000 to a 12-year low – excluding the 2020 pandemic.
The ‘jobs drought’ has been widely blamed on Labour making it increasingly expensive to hire by raising employer national insurance and sharply increasing the minimum wage.
Separate troubling data this week, revealing that the UK national debt has climbed above £3 trillion for the first time, illustrates the headache facing Healey as he tries to find the money to help households.
With bond markets watching closely for evidence of a plan to tackle the debt and UK ten-year borrowing costs already close to 19-year highs, the Chancellor cannot afford to splash out on unaffordable support packages.

items.title: Co-op and Circana extend data and insights tie up through new multi-year deal
items.summary: Circana and Co-op have announced a new multi-year agreement, extending a partnership that launched in 2020.Over the past few years, the former's HIVE portal has become a key part of Co-op’s data strategy, enabling the retailer and its suppliers to work from the same data and build a shared understan
items.body:
Circana and Co-op have announced a new multi-year agreement, extending a partnership that launched in 2020.
Over the past few years, the former's HIVE portal has become a key part of Co-op’s data strategy, enabling the retailer and its suppliers to work from the same data and build a shared understanding of customer behaviour, category performance and market trends.
HIVE brings together EPoS transactions, shopper insights, loyalty metrics, purchasing behaviours and market performance to provide a single view of performance across the business.
The renewed agreement marks the next phase of HIVE’s development, with the aim of strengthening Co-op’s ability to unlock value from its data assets while helping suppliers make faster, more informed decisions.
Over the next five years, Circana and Co-op will expand the platform’s capabilities through the integration of new data assets and measurement solutions, including supply chain, quick commerce and wholesale insights.
Imran Rasul, Chief Commercial Officer, Co-op, says: “We are delighted to deepen and extend our relationship with Circana. The next evolution of HIVE will provide suppliers with broader, more connected insights across our business, enabling faster decision-making, stronger collaboration and greater opportunities for shared growth. Together, we're creating a platform that helps turn data into action and supports long-term success for both Co-op and its partners.”
Cari Memmott, SVP Retail UK, Circana, says: “Circana is delighted to extend its partnership with Co-op through a new multi-year agreement. The renewal reflects the strength of our longstanding relationship and our shared commitment to driving growth through industry leading data, insights and technology. Together, we will continue to enhance collaboration between Co-op and its supplier partners while supporting initiatives that create lasting benefits for local communities.”

items.title: AI is everywhere at Foot Locker as Miniso goes large in London: this week's biggest retail technology stories
items.summary: It's Friday, the weekend is almost upon us, so let’s kick back and reflect on another eventful week for the retail tech space. Here's your briefing on the most important stories from the past few days, including Ikea UK, Matalan, Five Below, poq, Quorso, VoCoVo, AliExpress, Sensei, Muffato Group, Pr
items.body:
It's Friday, the weekend is almost upon us, so let’s kick back and reflect on another eventful week for the retail tech space. Here's your briefing on the most important stories from the past few days, including Ikea UK, Matalan, Five Below, poq, Quorso, VoCoVo, AliExpress, Sensei, Muffato Group, Primark, and Co-op.
1. Foot Locker teams with Stylitics as retailer taps AI technology to launch app-based closet builder solution
Foot Locker has developed, in partnership with Stylitics, a new AI powered closet builder, Fits, within its mobile app. In a LinkedIn post, Michael Cera, Interim Head of Product Management and Design at Foot Locker, said: “AI is everywhere. But, at Foot Locker, we challenged ourselves to think about how to improve and make positive change to our customers shopping experience through the use of AI.”
He added: “We engaged with customers, really listened, and in partnership with Stylitics, developed a key new closet builder within the Foot Locker app - let me introduce you to Fits! Start with something you own. Discover personalised outfits built around it. See those looks come to life on a virtual model.”
Customers can upload or take a photo of something they own, discover complete outfits built around it, and visualise those looks on a virtual model. Paired with a cart addition from the model view, the aim is to make purchasing a whole outfit styled around your own products that much easier.
Cera concluded: “This was a collaborative effort across Experience Design, Product Management, E-comm, Brand, and Stylitics, and came to life exactly as we all set out to do. Download or open your Foot Locker app today and give it a try!”
2. Miniso set to replace HMV on London's Oxford Street with opening of 19,000 sq ft flagship store
Miniso is gearing up to open its first Miniso Land store in the UK. The 19,000 sq ft flagship will be located at 363 Oxford Street, London, currently occupied by HMV, and will line up alongside the retailer’s other flagship stores, which includes New York’s Times Square and Paris’s Champs-Élysées, alongside over 8,300 stores globally.
Sam Foyle, Co-head of Global Retail at Savills, which acted for the landlord, says: “We’re seeing continued interest from brands for space on Oxford Street. Pedestrianisation plans have really fuelled momentum over the past year and, as the street enters a more mature stage of recovery, we expect this appetite to continue.”
“Oxford Street is a microcosm of the UK high street, where brands are increasingly focused on creating memorable, experience led destinations. Miniso Land is a great example of that trend, bringing an innovative flagship concept to one of the world’s most recognisable retail locations. Its decision to open at 363 Oxford Street is a strong vote of confidence in London and reinforces Oxford Street’s appeal as a destination for ambitious global brands.”
A Miniso spokesperson says: “London is an important part of our international growth, and bringing Miniso Land to Oxford Street marks an exciting next step. The flagship reflects our long-term commitment to the UK and our ambition to connect people with the characters and stories they love and bring joy to everyday life.”
Earlier this month, HMV announced it intended to vacate the site in March 2027 after three years. It first launched the Oxford Street site in 1921 and reopened it in late 2023 following a four-year absence.
3. Apadmi works with Matalan to build retailer's first fully native mobile app
Matalan reports that its first fully native app has recorded 1.76 million downloads since launching in August, with monthly active users growing by 10% month-on-month since go live. App orders increased 20% year-on-year in August and 28% in September, while conversion has reached 4.4%, ahead of its 3.4% target. Average order value is also 14% higher than on Matalan's website.
Developed in partnership with Apadmi, features include intelligent search to help customers find products more easily, richer product content and streamlined checkout through Apple Pay and Google Pay.
The app also brings Matalan Me rewards and account information together in one place, making it easier for customers to access their benefits and personalised offers.
It is designed to connect Matalan's digital and physical shopping experiences. An in-store barcode scanning feature allows customers to check product details, availability and reviews using their phones, helping them move more easily between shopping in-store and online.
4. AliExpress and YouTube expand affiliate partnership to four more markets following launch in South Korea
AliExpress has announced a partnership that brings its global product selection into YouTube’s creator ecosystem, giving eligible creators access to various products to feature in their content, along with new commission earning opportunities.
Following the launch of the collaboration in South Korea in March, the partnership will expand to four markets: the United States, Brazil, the United Kingdom and Germany. Further expansion will take place in phases, in line with the roll-out of YouTube’s affiliate programme in new markets.
With YouTube's recent extension of its Shopping Affiliate Programme to eligible creators in Germany and the United Kingdom, the partnership will connect participating creators not only in Europe but also eventually worldwide with AliExpress's product offerings. A particular focus is Brand+ - a dedicated selection of branded products from international and local brands.
Creators can discover and select AliExpress products directly within YouTube Studio. The integration connects AliExpress products with YouTube's three major content formats - long-form videos, shorts, and livestreams - allowing creators to tag shoppable product recommendations across key moments of audience discovery and engagement.
They can explore AliExpress's products across categories such as consumer electronics, sports and outdoor, home and living, and lifestyle. Using data on bestselling and trending products, they can handpick items that resonate with their audiences. Viewers can link directly from YouTube to AliExpress to complete their purchases.
5. US retailer Five Below taps poq platform for launch of new native iOS and Android mobile apps
poq has announced the launch of new native iOS and Android mobile apps for Five Below. Tiffany D’Amato, Vice President of Digital, Five Below, comments: “Our customers live on their phones, and these apps give them a faster, more engaging way to experience everything they love about Five Below.”
“Partnering with poq allowed us to bring that vision to life quickly and effectively, with a truly native experience built for our shoppers. We’re confident these apps will drive stronger customer engagement and long-term growth for the brand.”
Helen Slaven, Chief Revenue Officer at poq, says: “Five Below is exactly the kind of brand app commerce was made for, with a huge, engaged customer base and a shopping experience built on discovery. We are thrilled to partner with them to turn mobile into an owned channel that retains customers, grows lifetime value and scales with the business.”
A built-in price scanner lets shoppers scan an item in store and check its price and details on the spot, while personalised search helps customers explore the various products Five Below has to offer. Store aware features surface the nearest store and stock availability and push notifications, keep customers close to new arrivals and seasonal drops. The apps are built on poq’s platform and integrated with the Five Below commercetools commerce stack.
6. Quorso and VoCoVo among 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Best Retailer/Technology Supplier Relationship finalists
We’re pleased to announce the shortlist for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Best Retailer/Technology Supplier Relationship category. We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector.
Check out a rundown of our 2026 shortlists and finalists here.
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! It’s now over to our star studded judging panel who will decide the winners to be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.
Click here to book your place at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony on Wednesday, 4th November.
7. Co-op and Devon & Cornwall Police double retail crime cases solves with new reporting system roll-out
The partnership, according to those involved, delivers significantly faster justice for offences carried out, with data from Devon & Cornwall Police showing crimes reported through the platform - which is called SentrySIS - achieving a solve rate of almost 60%, which is approaching double the force’s average solve rate for retail crime versus retail crime being reported by those using traditional channels.
Data from Devon & Cornwall Police also revealed that 90% of identified shop theft offenders are repeat offenders, with just 50 individuals responsible for around a quarter of all shop theft offences in the Devon and Cornwall force area, often with more than 100 known offences each.
The new system enables stronger intelligence sharing; improved tracking of repeat offenders - connecting multiple offences committed by the same individual and building stronger cases against prolific offenders and, closer collaboration with police both at a local and central level.
Store colleagues upload incident details, CCTV, photos and impact statement enabling police to record and allocate the crime in as little 30 minutes - a process that could take police up to seven days. Furthermore, it removes the need for investigating officers to then approach the retailer for evidence, saving time for retailers and resulting in the average time taken for investigations to be completed and assigned an outcome being slashed by more than a third to 35 days.
The success of the pilot has seen the SentrySIS system, which links to Co-op’s wider partnership working with UK Partners Against Crime (UKPAC), now activated across all Co-op stores in Devon and Cornwall, with discussions now underway with additional police forces. Co-op’s own retail crime levels are falling with the retailer expected to see its lowest levels since the pandemic.
8. Ikea stumps up £31.5 million as it looks to make UK fulfilment more efficient and reduce packaging waste
Ikea UK is investing £31.5 million across its Peterborough and Doncaster customer distribution centres (CDC) as the retailer aims to make online fulfilment more efficient and sustainable.
In Peterborough, new technology is packaging customer orders to size and reducing material usage by up to 30%, by preventing waste from oversized boxes and filling paper. In Doncaster, Ikea is trialling a new regional fulfilment capability, serving customers in the north and Scotland from a closer location to them.
The investments will strengthen Ikea’s UK fulfilment network as online sales account for 43.3% of total UK sales in financial year 2026. It is investing £30 million in new technology for its Peterborough CDC, with the upgrades taking place over a two-year period. As part of this, it has launched new PackSize technology to prevent waste from oversized cardboard boxes and filling materials by packaging customer orders to size. On average, the technology reduces material usage by up to 30% and void fill by up to 60%.
The technology is expected to increase the share of parcels processed through automation at the Peterborough CDC from 47% today to 75% in 2027, helping the fulfilment team prepare orders for delivery more efficiently. These additional orders would otherwise have been packaged by manually creating a packing carton which includes having to measure the article then creating the cartons to fit the order. Three drones and nests were introduced at the site in January to support inventory management. They scan each aisle in short cycles, helping Ikea to keep stock in the right place and meet customer demand.
Ikea is investing £1.5 million in trialling a new fulfilment capability at its Doncaster CDC. The site now fulfils orders for customers in the Gateshead, Edinburgh and Glasgow areas, with plans for Sheffield to follow. By fulfilling these orders from Doncaster rather than Peterborough, Ikea expects to reduce emissions from delivery journeys by an estimated 280 tonnes of CO2 annually. The new capability has created an additional 80 jobs at the Doncaster site.
9. Sensei looks to take retail intelligence beyond the store checkout as it teams with Brazil’s Muffato Group
Sensei has deployed its technology in a new Muffato Go store in Curitiba, Brazil. This has been developed in partnership with supermarket specialist Grupo Muffato.
While Sensei first became known for its autonomous store technology, it says that the intelligence behind those stores has always been designed to address a broader challenge: giving physical retail the ability and the data to understand and automate its own operations in real-time.
The new Muffato Go, according to those involved, will put that capability into practice, showing how the same underlying technology can improve shelf availability, detect losses, automate checkout, manage fresh products and support online order fulfillment.
Headquartered in Portugal and operating across Europe and Brazil, Sensei has deployed its technology in more than 100 autonomous points of sale, including the world's largest autonomous store, opened in Leiria, Portugal, in 2025.
“The new Muffato Go shows what AI can already do in a physical store. Shoppers get a faster, simpler way to buy, but that is only the visible part. Our models recognise products and shopper interactions as they happen, and store teams get the right task at the right time," says Vasco Portugal, CEO and Co-founder at Sensei.
"The real value is turning what happens in the store into intelligence that supports the entire business, from the shop floor to the head office. That is what we mean by Conscious Spaces: physical spaces that see, understand and act."
10. Primark announces AI powered supply chain decision capability partnership with Kallikor
Primark has partnered with Kallikor to introduce a simulation led approach to supply chain decisions. The aim being for the retailer to test and validate operational and capital changes before implementation.
The tie up begins with creating digital twins of Primark’s distribution centres, allowing teams to test alternative operating configurations before implementation.
By comparing scenarios in a simulated environment, the retailer says it can identify more efficient approaches while protecting customer service and avoiding downstream cost or operational impacts across the store estate.
Adam Hoccom, Director of Supply Chain at Primark, says: “As we continue to grow across markets, ensuring our supply chain is designed to support that ambition is critical."
"A key part of that is making sure our distribution centres operate efficiently while remaining aligned to store needs. Working with Kallikor allows us to test and compare different operating configurations - from layout and flow changes within sites to broader network considerations - before we commit capital spend."
"This gives us greater confidence in the choices we make and how they will perform in practice, strengthening our ability to innovate and make well informed decisions as we evolve our network.”

items.title: Bodycare and PMC shortlisted at 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards for AI first, experience led store push
items.summary: Bodycare and PMC have been shortlisted in two categories at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards for their partnership in designing and delivering the digital infrastructure powering the value led health and beauty retailer’s new store network.Named as finalists in both the Bricks and Mortar and AI Innov
items.body:
Bodycare and PMC have been shortlisted in two categories at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards for their partnership in designing and delivering the digital infrastructure powering the value led health and beauty retailer’s new store network.
Named as finalists in both the Bricks and Mortar and AI Innovation (UK) categories, the partnership has been recognised for bringing cutting-edge innovation and live AI use cases to physical retail environments.
As Bodycare continues its high street comeback at pace, having already opened five stores in Sheffield, Derby, Leicester, Bradford and Dudley, its partnership with PMC is bringing its vision of a connected, immersive and AI first store estate to life.
Blending commerce and experiences in-store, Bodycare now runs all store operations through its proprietary, custom built AI platform, AIMEE, which connects data across customers, inventory, trends, social content and store performance to continually improve decision-making.
Each store also features a dedicated, free-to-use content production studio, allowing creators and micro-influencers to generate hyper-localised content that drives community engagement, as well as informing inventory allocation based on live demand signals. Since July, Bodycare has onboarded 673 creators, generating 7.5 million views across its creator network content.
To enable this vision, PMC designed and delivered Bodycare’s digital architecture from the ground up, creating the connected infrastructure required to support its extensive in-store technology ecosystem.
This included deploying PMC’s Graphene Engage platform to power traditional, mobile and self-service checkout experiences, alongside its Interact digital display solution, which turns screens across the estate into interactive customer touchpoints.
“We’re thrilled to have been shortlisted in two RTIH Innovation Awards,” says Bodycare’s CMO, Tash Courtenay-Smith. “From the hugely positive reaction from communities where we’ve opened new stores to the viral buzz being driven online by our content creator network, this recognition from the RTIH Awards marks another milestone in bringing Bodycare back to the high street.”
“Bodycare is bringing value led beauty back to the high street with a bang, proving what a bold vision, powered by technology and communities, can achieve,” says Elliott Winskill, Technology & Solutions Director at PMC, who is also acting as Technical Lead for Bodycare.
“To be recognised by the RTIH Innovation Awards - a hallmark of innovation excellence in the industry - for helping create a new blueprint for bricks and mortar retailing is further validation of the momentum behind Bodycare’s comeback.”

items.title: Fed questions whether falling shop theft figures tell the full story
items.summary: The Federation of Independent Retailers (the Fed) has questioned whether the latest government figures accurately reflect the true scale of shop theft, warning that recorded offences do not tell the full story of the crime experienced by independent retailers. The latest figures issued by the… This story continues at Fed questions whether falling shop theft figures tell the full story Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The latest figures issued by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) show that recorded shop theft fell by 2% in the year ending June 2026, with 519,516 offences compared with 530,336 the previous year.
National president Hemanshu Patel said: “While the figures show a fall in recorded shop theft, we need to understand whether this reflects a genuine reduction in crime or whether it also reflects the difficulties retailers face when reporting incidents and the lack of confidence some have in the process.
“More than half a million recorded offences in a single year remains a serious concern. Behind these figures are independent retailers dealing with repeated theft, intimidation and the financial and emotional impact of crime. The wider impact on staff, customers and local communities must not be overlooked.”
In a statement issued by the Home Office, policing minister Sarah Jones said: “Police are taking this crime seriously, and with more officers patrolling town centres and responding to these incidents we can have a real impact.
“Shop theft charge rates rose from 19% to 24%. This is still too low, and we want to see this figure continue to climb. We will continue this trend by pushing ahead with plans to strengthen local policing.”
Patel added: “We welcome the minister’s recognition that shop theft charge rates remain too low. However, retailers need to see meaningful action on the ground, not simply changes in the statistics.
“Reporting crime must be straightforward, police responses must be appropriate and offenders must understand there are consequences for their actions. Retailers should not have to navigate unnecessary red tape only to feel that little is being done.
“We also want the government to consider a dedicated retail crime grant scheme to help independent retailers improve security and protect their businesses.
“Recorded figures are only part of the picture. Independent retailers deserve to feel safe, supported and properly protected.”

items.title: Sainsbury’s grows faster than Tesco in H1, but its sales momentum is fading, says GlobalData
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Following today’s release of Sainsbury’s figures for the 28 weeks ending 12 September 2026; Eleanor Simpson-Gould, senior retail analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “Sainsbury’s has outpaced Tesco on sales growth in H1, but weak non-food sales continue to hold back an otherwise strong food performance. Sales from continuing […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Following today’s release of Sainsbury’s figures for the 28 weeks ending 12 September 2026; Eleanor Simpson-Gould, senior retail analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “Sainsbury’s has outpaced Tesco on sales growth in H1, but weak non-food sales continue to hold back an otherwise strong food performance. Sales from continuing operations (excluding fuel) rose 2.6% to £14.0bn, driven by a 4.3% rise in fresh food sales and continued trade-up to Taste the Difference. Like-for-like (l-f-l) sales rose 1.9%, ahead of Tesco’s 1.5%. However, momentum slowed sharply through the first half, from 2.3% in Q1 to 1.2% in Q2, against tough comparatives and easing food inflation. Sainsbury’s raised the lower end of its full-year underlying operating profit guidance to £1,025m, matching Tesco’s cautious upgrade earlier this month. Shares fell close to 4% in morning trading, likely reflecting this caution alongside plans to keep investing in value, quality, availability and service through a very competitive second half.
“The agreed sale of Argos to Swift Partners is the defining change of the half. Argos, now a discontinued operation, saw sales fall 1.8% in H1, worsening to a 2.7% decline in Q2. Big-ticket furniture sales stalled in the heatwave, and the move away from legacy Argos credit cards weighed on sales. Selling Argos removes a volatile drag for the grocer and will free Sainsbury’s to focus capital and strategy on food, but non-food will remain a weak spot. Sainsbury’s general merchandise and clothing sales decreased by 3.4%, largely due to a deliberate shift of space towards food. The 13% rise in toy sales after a range reset shows that fewer, better ranges can still grow sales going into the gifting season. However, Argos will still trade this Christmas under Sainsbury’s ownership, so a weak golden quarter will further hamper Sainsbury’s performance. Sainsbury’s must keep the separation, due in February 2029, tightly managed so that it does not distract from the core business.
“Grocery sales rose 2.9% to £13.2bn, with Aldi Price Match and Nectar Prices on almost 11,000 products driving growth in the half. Premium remains central to growth. Taste the Difference sales grew by more than 6%, and the restaurant-quality Discovery range doubled, driving a quarter of that growth. With the Middle East conflict continuing to put pressure on energy costs and inflation set to rise into Sainsbury’s H2, the grocer must protect volumes over Christmas and retain focus on price matching. It should lead with fewer, higher-impact Discovery and Taste the Difference festive lines and use Nectar Prices to lower the barrier to trying them.”

items.title: Tax online sales more heavily to save high streets, Burnham urged
items.summary: Exclusive: British Chambers of Commerce president calls for overhaul of business rates and greater powers for local leaders How Middleton’s revival could inspire struggling towns What makes a good town? Here are five key ingredients Andy Burnham has been urged by one of his most senior former advisers to tax internet sales more heavily than in-store purchases to help “level the playing field” for struggling high streets. As the prime minister and his chancellor, John Healey, prepare for their first budget next week, Andy Haldane joined calls for action to stop more shops closing across the UK. Continue reading...
items.body:
Andy Burnham has been urged by one of his most senior former advisers to tax internet sales more heavily than in-store purchases to help “level the playing field” for struggling high streets.
As the prime minister and his chancellor, John Healey, prepare for their first budget next week, Andy Haldane joined calls for action to stop more shops closing across the UK.
In an interview for a Guardian series looking at how Britain can reverse the declining fortunes of towns, the former Bank of England chief economist urged them to launch a realignment of the tax system away from favouring online sellers, alongside a review of business rates and measures to turbocharge devolution.
“The balance of tax incentives are strongly skewed towards the digital over the physical, and the large over small, and if you’re serious about high streets that needs somehow rebalancing,” he said.
Calling on Burnham to follow through with Labour’s manifesto promise to “replace” the business rates system, Haldane said “some levelling of the playing field” was needed to help smaller operators who faced soaring costs and evaporating demand.
“One of the reasons why high streets are dying, and some of the towns, is business rates are punitive for smaller shops,” he said. “This needs to be wrapped up with that more fundamental review of business rates and I’ll hope we see that in the budget.
The prime minister has made town centres a top priority after years of decline that have left many hollowed-out, with shops closed, buildings boarded up and once-busy hubs sitting empty.
Healey’s budget on Wednesday is tipped to include measures to ease the pressure on these high streets, including a tax crackdown on online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay. The measure could raise up to an extra £1bn by forcing them to collect VAT on behalf of large-scale sellers based in the UK as well as those overseas.
He is also expected to honour the promise Burnham made in June to take more small players out of the system altogether by raising the rent valuation threshold at which businesses start paying.
The Treasury is also understood to have taken an interest in a report by the IPPR thinktank calling for an online sales tax to fund lower high street business rates. Big retailers including Morrisons, Waterstones and the UK’s biggest supermarket, Tesco, have long called for such a move.
Labour has already had one business rates shake-up. In April, taxes on warehouses used by online retailers were increased, but the increase on the UK’s most valuable commercial properties also drew other large buildings such as department stores and hotels fuelling calls for further tweaks. Some retailers have warned against a more targeted warehouse tax because many big chains now combine online shopping with a high-street presence.
Allen Simpson, the boss of the trade body UKHospitality, said the government had indicated it would ease costs on his sector, but he sensed ministers were wary of US retribution if taxes on big US-based tech firms such as Amazon and eBay were hit, warning that “Trump might hit us with a tariff”.
Burnham’s push to revive communities with measures to hand more power and money to local leaders comes as Nigel Farage’s Reform UK seeks to weaponise high-street decline. Research shows public support for his rightwing populist party has grown most in the places where high-street vacancy rates have risen most.
Haldane, who is the president of the British Chambers of Commerce, advised Burnham as he prepared to enter Downing Street but did not take a formal position in government.
A leading expert in regional economic development who masterminded Boris Johnson’s levelling up plans – before distancing himself from the Conservatives over cuts to local government – he praised Burnham’s agenda to hand more power and funding to local leaders. However, Haldane said a revamp of business rates would be critical to boosting the economies of struggling towns. “That would be a very, very important element of the ‘growth in every postcode’, and making the most of devolution outside the city centric mayoralties,” he said.
In his first weeks in power Burnham announced a cut in business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April. Labour has also introduced community ownership funds and launched a £5.8bn “pride in place” strategy to hand more money and power to local leaders to support regeneration.
However, retail and hospitality industry leaders argue that Labour has added to the headwinds facing high streets by increasing taxes on employment and adding to other business costs, and have pressed for these to be partly reversed to fund youth job creation.
As ministers prepare to publish a refreshed high streets strategy, polling by researchers at More in Common shared with the Guardian by the campaign group Power to Change shows the extent of the challenge.
Whereas most people describe their local area warmly, opinions typically turn negative when asked about their high street, with words like “empty”, “run down,” “tired” and “declining” common.
As many as six in 10 think handing more power to community organisations, residents or local businesses would help to improve their high street. As few as 15% thought the government would make better decisions.
Haldane urged Labour to hand more powers to directly elected mayors – including the eventual responsibility for setting local rates of income tax, national insurance and VAT. “Other countries have cracked the code on this. So there’s no reason why we couldn’t or shouldn’t,” he said.
Healey is preparing to use the budget to unveil plans to allow mayors to retain a share of income tax but is expected to stop short of handing over the responsibilities from the Treasury to set local rates.
A Treasury spokesperson said: “We are on the side of businesses. The chancellor is giving the high street more breathing space, cutting business rates by 20% for pubs, social clubs and live music venues. This is alongside £4.3bn to limit bill rises, funded by a higher tax rate for big online warehouses, and capping corporation tax.
“As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

items.title: How Middleton’s revival could be grist to the mill for Britain’s struggling towns
items.summary: Turnaround initiated by Andy Burnham and led by Steve Coogan could provide blueprint for other neglected areas Save high street by taxing online sales at higher rate, Burnham urged What makes a good town? Here are five key ingredients The former England footballer Paul Scholes and the actor Steve Coogan stare out from beside a fish and chip shop in Middleton, near Manchester . Looming over a mural of the pair – and the whole town – is an enormous former cotton mill that powered its economy a century ago. The deafening looms and spindles of Warwick Mill fell silent decades ago, replaced in recent years by TikTok “urban explorers” who share videos of themselves crawling through its abandoned shell. Continue reading...
items.body:
The former England footballer Paul Scholes and the actor Steve Coogan stare out from beside a fish and chip shop in Middleton, near Manchester. Looming over a mural of the pair – and the whole town – is an enormous former cotton mill that powered its economy a century ago.
The deafening looms and spindles of Warwick Mill fell silent decades ago, replaced in recent years by TikTok “urban explorers” who share videos of themselves crawling through its abandoned shell.
Yet the old building may have life inside it yet: last month Rochdale council wrestled Warwick Mill out of the hands of its absentee owner, a millionaire Chinese businessman, under whom it had been derelict for years.
Now the Grade II-listed site is at the centre of plans Andy Burnham believes could turn Middleton, where he was once a trainee journalist, into a blueprint for the future of Britain’s struggling towns.
“It used to be good,” said Dorothy Kersh, in the town square with her husband, Ernie, both 83. “In the 70s we had a cinema, we had banks. It’s lost character and we’ve hardly got any shops. We haven’t even got a bank now – I never thought NatWest would leave Middleton. It’s just going downhill.”
A few miles between Manchester and Rochdale, Middleton is typical of the existential crisis suffered by most British towns.
A decade or so ago, locals could find virtually everything they needed in its neat square of grocers, butchers and banks. But a giant Tesco has hoovered up the cash since it opened in 2013, compounding the rise of online and out-of-town shopping.
The town of about 50,000 people has lost all its banks and, days before Burnham became prime minister, the remains of its post office were closed by Modella Capital, the new private equity owner of WH Smith.
Now the shopping precinct offers little more than bookmakers, vape stores, pawnbrokers and fast-food outlets.
Even its geographic identity feels muddled. Middleton was historically in Lancashire but the town has a Manchester postcode and dial code, although residents pay their council tax to Rochdale. The region’s lauded tram network does not stop here.
“It’s really a dying town,” said Tim King, outside a large post office branch that closed down years ago. “We’ve only got one cash machine and that’s at Tesco, and there’s never any money in it. We’ve lost out on the trams. We haven’t got anything down here, to be honest.”
But six miles from the birthplace of the modern co-operative movement in 1844, a community fightback is under way.
Months before he departed for Downing Street, Burnham launched a mayoral development corporation for Middleton, giving local leaders power to set lower business rates, acquire underused land and property, and build 1,500 new homes.
The body is led by Coogan, the Bafta-winning creator of Alan Partridge, and Rose Marley, the chief executive of Co-operatives UK. Crucially, residents and business owners will have a seat at the table: a survey of 2,000 Middletonians is shaping the agenda of this new mayoral body – with Warwick Mill and other empty buildings identified by locals as an immediate priority.
Wearing a hard hat and hi-vis vest during a tour of Warwick Mill last month, Coogan said the Middleton of his childhood was a “thriving” town but that “over the last 35 years there has been a kind of a bank ride” by firms registered in the British Virgin Islands, China and the US: “All that money has been extracted but very little has been put back into the infrastructure.”
Coogan said the project was about more than attempting to revitalise his home town. It was a chance to reverse the political and economic malaise that has seen former Labour voters shift to rightwing populist parties such as Reform UK in post-industrial areas across Britain.
“There’s a problem in this country which is post-industrial neglect,” he told the Guardian. “The idea, the Blairite approach: it’s called multinationalism, there is nothing we can do, throw your hands up, you’ve just got to see what happens, we can’t help these people.
“Leaving that vacuum will mean that the extremists, populist extremists, will fill that gap. That’s the problem with top-down, well-meaning, but disempowering, philanthropic, centralised socialism. People don’t want to receive charity, they want to be empowered.”
Coogan is part of a group called Middleton Co-operating, which aims to “rewire the whole of the economy locally” by taking infrastructure and everyday essentials into public control.
Its plans include using renewable energy, like solar panels and small wind turbines, to help power a secondary school and a hospice. A trial involving heat pumps and solar panels on a terrace of Edwardian homes is also being put together.
Banks could soon return too, with plans for a banking hub where Lloyds, NatWest and others could open on different days of the week, alongside financial advisers.
The group, which was backed by Burnham when he was mayor and in June won £4.5m funding from the national lottery’s solidarity fund, wants to expand into food production, early years support, mental health provision and adult social care.
“These are all things that have the biggest impact on people’s day-to-day lives and they’re generally all owned by big business and private equity – they cost too much and are a cause of a lot of stress in the community,” said Mark Fraser, a founder of Middleton Co-operating.
Earlier this year, an arts venue run by Middleton Co-operating was forced out of the town’s sprawling shopping centre – which was owned by two London-based real estate companies and incorporated in the British Virgin Islands – as it could not afford the £43,000-a-year rent and service charge demanded by the landlord. In its place a pawnbroker moved in on a 10-year lease.
“It was a bit of a sickener,” said Fraser. “It was a lesson in that they were saying they loved what we were doing for the community, but when it came to it what counts is the bottom line.”
Even with Coogan’s star power and the prime minister’s backing, the scale of the challenge is huge.
Warwick Mill is an utter wreck and could cost tens of millions of pounds to bring back to life. To Fraser, it is a symbol of a town where people feel “neglected and forgotten”, and most had lost hope in its future.
“The cost of rescuing and converting something of that size is colossal,” said Tim Heatley, the co-founder of property firm Capital & Centric, which specialises in turning unloved old buildings – such as former mills and even multistorey car parks – into sought-after homes.
It was a 7pm telephone call from Burnham that turned Heatley on to Warwick Mill in January this year.
The then mayor told Heatley he had seen Capital & Centric’s renovation of the dilapidated Weir Mill in Stockport and asked him to take a look at the Middleton site.
As it happened, Heatley had already been in contact with Kam Lei Fong, the Macau-based developer who owned Warwick Mill. But with Burnham on board, the project accelerated.
“For me, the opportunity is much bigger than doing a nice conversion of an old mill,” he said. “Warwick is absolutely colossal and has loomed over Middleton for more than a century. If we can fill it with life again, it has the potential to become an anchor for the town … and give confidence for investment to follow around it.
“The challenge now is turning all that momentum into an actual place, getting Warwick fixed up, full of people and properly part of Middleton again. Ideally before Andy’s next career move leaves us needing to find somebody else to cut the ribbon.”

items.title: Supermarket giants welcome crackdown on Aldi and Lidl
items.summary: Supermarket giants, including Waitrose and Morrisons, have welcomed the competition watchdog’s decision to crack down on Aldi and Lidl. Lidl and Aldi are currently excluded from a law which bans the UK’s biggest supermarket chains from engaging in so-called ‘landblocking‘. Top grocers have already warned that the existing rules allowed the two German discounters to use a “problematic” [...]
items.body:
Supermarket giants welcome crackdown on Aldi and Lidl
Supermarket giants, including Waitrose and Morrisons, have welcomed the competition watchdog’s decision to crack down on Aldi and Lidl.
Lidl and Aldi are currently excluded from a law which bans the UK’s biggest supermarket chains from engaging in so-called ‘landblocking‘. Top grocers have already warned that the existing rules allowed the two German discounters to use a “problematic” loophole to block rivals from opening nearby.
However, the competition regulator is now set to force the two grocers to comply.
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) on Thursday confirmed its provisional decision to extend the Controlled Land Order to cover Aldi and Lidl.
The pair had previously been excluded from the rules because they were classed as “limited assortment discounters”. But the CMA has said it will now categorise the two firms as “large grocery retailers” because of their rapid expansion in recent years.
Lidl and Aldi will join Asda, Co-op, Marks & Spencer, Morrisons, Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Waitrose in being blocked from using these land laws to gain an advantage over their rivals.
Budget supermarket Iceland, which is not covered by the land order, welcomed the CMA’s provisional decision.
In a letter to the regulator, published on Thursday, the company said existing rules allowed Aldi and Lidl to “deploy problematic land arrangements […] at scale and in a way that could have a material adverse impact on competition for groceries across the UK market”.
Though the two German discounters occupied a relatively small part of the UK’s grocery market when the Controlled Land Order was set up, the firms “now each exert a significant and compelling degree of competitive influence in the UK grocery market,” Iceland said.
Lidl and Aldi ‘shielded from competition’
Grocers Morrisons, Waitrose and Iceland each wrote to the CMA, expressing concerns that Lidl and Aldi are preparing to expand further in the UK, citing plans to reach 1,500 stores each.
Aldi and Lidl have previously claimed they should not be classed as large grocery retailers because they offer fewer products than their rivals.
But Morrisons told the CMA that both supermarket chains “publicly market their product range as being suitable for a full weekly shop” and pose “intense competition” even in the categories they claim to be weak in.
A Waitrose spokesperson wrote to the regulator, warning that it had seen “first hand” Lidl’s use of the land order to “restrict the ability of other grocery retailers to open new stores and shield Lidl from local competition”.
The up-market grocer said the CMA should impose its rulings as soon as possible. “It is important that these decisions are taken without further delay to ensure there is equal opportunity in the competition between LGRs and Aldi and Lidl to secure further sites for grocery retail.”
Juliette Enser, executive director for competition enforcement at the regulator, said the new rules will “help level the playing field and make sure shoppers get the best choice of products and prices in their area”.
Responding to the CMA’s provisional ruling in August, Lidl and Aldi said the crackdown would not slow their plans to expand rapidly in the UK.
Commenting on the decision, an Aldi spokesperson said: “We remain firmly committed to opening hundreds of new stores across the country, bringing Aldi’s unbeatable value and award-winning quality to even more customers.
A Lidl spokesperson said: “As a discounter, we have always welcomed and embraced competition within the market, and our focus remains on continuing to open new stores and bringing our high-quality, lowest-priced groceries to even more communities.”

items.title: Primark announces AI powered supply chain decision capability partnership with Kallikor
items.summary: Primark has partnered with Kallikor to introduce a simulation led approach to supply chain decisions. The aim being for the retailer to test and validate operational and capital changes before implementation.The tie up begins with creating digital twins of Primark’s distribution centres, allowing te
items.body:
Primark has partnered with Kallikor to introduce a simulation led approach to supply chain decisions. The aim being for the retailer to test and validate operational and capital changes before implementation.
The tie up begins with creating digital twins of Primark’s distribution centres, allowing teams to test alternative operating configurations before implementation.
By comparing scenarios in a simulated environment, the retailer says it can identify more efficient approaches while protecting customer service and avoiding downstream cost or operational impacts across the store estate.
Adam Hoccom, Director of Supply Chain at Primark, says: “As we continue to grow across markets, ensuring our supply chain is designed to support that ambition is critical."
"A key part of that is making sure our distribution centres operate efficiently while remaining aligned to store needs. Working with Kallikor allows us to test and compare different operating configurations - from layout and flow changes within sites to broader network considerations - before we commit capital spend."
"This gives us greater confidence in the choices we make and how they will perform in practice, strengthening our ability to innovate and make well-informed decisions as we evolve our network.”
By modelling operational flows in detail - from pick paths and labour constraints to throughput variability and service impacts - Primark can see how proposed changes will perform in practice before they are introduced. The models are built from its operational data, with the aim of ensuring outcomes reflect how the system actually performs under a range of real operating conditions rather than relying on assumptions or averaged views of the network.
The modelling also establishes a living decision environment built on Primark’s operational data that can be reused and extended as new strategic questions arise. Rather than commissioning a new analysis for each decision, teams can continuously test alternatives within the same validated model as the supply chain evolves.
Through simulation and AI enabled scenario exploration, they can run and compare multiple operating futures side-by-side, assessing trade offs across cost, service, capacity and risk in parallel.
Jack O’Connell, CEO and Co-Founder at Kallikor, says: “At Primark’s scale, no supply chain decision exists in isolation. A change in one distribution centre can affect capacity, flow, service and performance across the wider network. Our role is to help teams explore decisions that would otherwise carry too much uncertainty, testing different scenarios before implementation so leaders can understand the trade-offs and move forward with confidence."
"We’re proud to support Primark as they build a simulation led decision-making capability, beginning with their distribution centres and creating the foundations for better decisions across the wider supply chain over time.”
While the initial focus is on distribution centre configuration, the modelling environment is designed to be reused as new questions arise, allowing teams to test automation pathways, capital investments, network design changes and future growth scenarios within the same validated system.
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
Supply chain technology will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards, which celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world, have now closed for entries. Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
Check out our 2026 shortlists and finalists here.
We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector.
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! It’s now over to our star studded judging panel who will decide the winners to be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.
