items.body:
John Lewis has announced a major expansion of its rapid delivery service alongside significant website and mobile app enhancements. By partnering with Deliveroo and Uber Eats, the retailer is making approximately 10,000 products available in as little as 30 minutes to customers within the catchment area of eight stores across London and select home counties – including Oxford Street, Peter Jones, Welwyn Garden City, Bluewater, and Kingston. This strategic move strengthens John Lewis’s omnichannel footprint, seamlessly integrating speed and convenience to its physical and digital retail approach.
Marking 25 years since johnlewis.com first launched, John Lewis is investing in both physical shops and its online platforms to inspire and serve customers however they choose to shop. By combining in-store customer service and Partner expertise with an inspirational website, powerful app, extensive click and collect network including next day collection from nearly 16,000 locations including Waitrose stores, and fast online delivery options, the retailer is bringing the very best of its shops and digital channels together as part of its multi-year £800m transformation programme.
Rapid delivery complements John Lewis’s established standard delivery and nationwide click and collect network, giving customers an ultra-fast delivery option for last-minute needs, urgent tech replacements, or emergency gifts. Data from the trial highlights a strong lunchtime peak, with 12pm to 2pm emerging as the highest-volume period for sales, driven by demand for urgent tech items, emergency gifts, and treat purchases.
The most popular item bought via the rapid delivery pilot to date is the Sony PlayStation 5 Controller, with gifting items and gifting packaging featuring highly, as well as personal fans as customers reached for a must-have cool down over the summer months.
To support its omnichannel focus and help prepare for peak trading – where up to 150,000 online orders a day will be processed – John Lewis is introducing a suite of digital enhancements across JohnLewis.com and its mobile app. These improvements make it easier and quicker for customers to find and buy what they need, as well as offering relevant inspiration and ideas based on their browsing history.
Digital upgrades across the website and mobile app are designed to improve and simplify the overall customer experience. With a fresh look and feel, the website now offers customers more content and inspiration, and upgraded site search helps shoppers quickly find what they are looking for. The app, which now accounts for approximately 40% of online sales, continues to play a central role in driving customer engagement. It includes easy access to My John Lewis rewards and benefits, order history, and Live Chat to enable customers to access any support that they need.
To further enhance convenience and support modern shopping habits, John Lewis is embracing AI-powered discovery. With traffic from digital assistants continuing to grow year-on-year, the retailer is ensuring product ranges are easily discoverable and is currently developing a brand-new AI-powered product finder set to launch in time for Christmas.
Demonstrating how physical stores and online platforms work together as part of a seamless omnichannel strategy, John Lewis has delivered over 1.3 million items directly from its shops to customers since scaling deliver-from-store, unlocking local store stock to fulfill online orders and helping customers purchase items that would have traditionally been shown as out of stock online.
Dom McBrien, chief digital and omnichannel officer at John Lewis, said: “Bringing the best of John Lewis into our customers’ daily lives is at the heart of our transformation. Whether shoppers are seeking expert advice from Partners in our stores, picking up an order via click and collect, or ordering via our Deliveroo or Uber Eats for delivery in 30 minutes, we are meeting them wherever they are with trusted quality and exceptional service. By expanding our rapid delivery option alongside major website upgrades, we are giving customers ultimate convenience and flexibility without ever compromising on the service they expect from John Lewis.”
Jeff Wemyss, general manager for Deliveroo in the UK and Ireland, said: “We are thrilled to bring such a well-respected British retailer onto our platform as we continue to build a new destination for shopping. Whether it is last-minute homeware for a dinner party, a gift for a friend or simply a spontaneous treat, our partnership with John Lewis gives you a department store in your pocket.”
Merve Basci, general manager for Uber Eats in the UK said, “John Lewis is a British icon, and after joining forces last summer, we’re thrilled to play a part in their 25-year digital journey. Retail on Uber Eats is skyrocketing as customers turn to rapid delivery for everything from emergency tech to gifts or treats, and we love bringing the modern magic of John Lewis straight to customers’ doors.”
The John Lewis website launched in 2001 with 5,000 stocked products, around 1,000 daily orders, and 800,000 daily page impressions, and its first sale was a beech salt and pepper mill for £22.85. Today in 2026, the website offers over 300,000 products, handles an average of 55,000 daily orders, and generates an average of 1.6 million daily page impressions.

items.title: The new digital consumer: convenience, personalisation and trust
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. The retail landscape continues to evolve rapidly, shaped by changing consumer expectations and technological advances. Modern shoppers are more digitally connected than ever, which enables them to access a world of products and services at their fingertips. The rise of the new digital consumer is transforming how retailers operate, highlighting three key themes: convenience, personalisation, […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
The retail landscape continues to evolve rapidly, shaped by changing consumer expectations and technological advances. Modern shoppers are more digitally connected than ever, which enables them to access a world of products and services at their fingertips. The rise of the new digital consumer is transforming how retailers operate, highlighting three key themes: convenience, personalisation, and trust.
Seamless convenience: the non-negotiable standard
Convenience is now the cornerstone of digital retail. Shoppers expect fast, frictionless experiences from start to finish, browsing, purchasing, delivery, and returns. Mobile devices have made shopping possible anywhere and anytime, removing the traditional boundaries of opening hours and physical locations. Retailers that focus on streamlining processes, such as providing one-click checkouts or same-day delivery, create an environment where interruptions are minimised and satisfaction is maximised.
Technological integrations play a big role in creating such convenience. From automated chatbots that provide immediate assistance, to real-time inventory updates, digital solutions offer clarity and support at every step. The expectation for consistency across channels is also significant. Whether a customer interacts via an app or visits a physical shop, seamless integration and a unified experience are essential. For retailers, this means investing in backend infrastructure and continually iterating services to meet the ever-climbing baseline set by today’s digital consumers.
Personalisation: tailoring the experience
As digital natives become the mainstream shopper demographic, personalisation has shifted from a novelty to a necessity. Consumers now expect brands to understand their preferences and deliver relevant recommendations, communications, and offers. These experiences range from customised product suggestions to targeted promotions based on previous activity. Similar personalisation features appear across many digital services, including sports betting, where users may encounter content tailored to their interests. Artificial intelligence and advanced analytics help businesses predict what customers might want next, subtly guiding their journey and increasing engagement.
Effective personalisation goes beyond just algorithms. It also accounts for context, mood, and intent, carefully balancing data-driven insights with an understanding of the broader customer journey. Privacy considerations are, however, intimately linked to personalisation. Digital consumers appreciate tailored content, but they are also acutely aware of how their data is collected and used. Transparent communication about data practices and intuitive privacy controls are essential to foster trust while delivering a bespoke experience.
The foundation of trust in the digital age
Trust is more critical now than ever for digital retailers. Consumers share vast amounts of information online, from delivery addresses to purchasing habits, and they want reassurance that this data is handled safely and ethically. Reports of cyber-attacks, data breaches, and misuse of personal information have made today’s digital shopper more cautious. Retailers must instil confidence by implementing robust security measures and being upfront about how consumer data is managed.
Beyond data protection, trust extends to the reliability of products and services. Shoppers look for consistent quality, authentic reviews, and genuine engagement. Transparency in communication, particularly regarding returns or refunds, as well as clarity around sourcing and sustainability, further cements loyalty. A single negative experience can significantly impact reputation, so retailers must proactively listen and respond to consumer feedback to maintain trust in an ever-more competitive digital market.
Navigating the digital consumer mindset
The new digital consumer is knowledgeable, selective, and values their time and privacy. Retailers who prioritise convenience, develop meaningful personalisation strategies, and demonstrate a strong commitment to trust are best positioned to thrive. The continuous evolution of technology and behaviour means that adaptability is essential; what delights a shopper today may be standard practice tomorrow. In this landscape, the brands that succeed are those that listen closely, engage genuinely, and innovate responsibly, ensuring they meet the needs of digital consumers both now and in the future.
Industry leaders continue to observe and respond to these trends, creating services that mirror consumers’ lives and anticipating preferences even before a need arises. As digital adoption deepens, the interplay between convenience, personalisation, and trust will remain at the forefront of retail innovation, shaping purchase journeys worldwide.

items.title: Mike Ashley’s Frasers loosens grip on Burberry
items.summary: Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group has loosened its grip on Burberry, despite ramping up its pursuit of high-fashion names. The retail giant, which owns Sports Direct and Flannels, had built up a position in Burberry over recent weeks but has now faltered in its pursuit of the group.  Frasers Group had increased its position in Burberry [...]
items.body:
Mike Ashley’s Frasers loosens grip on Burberry
Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group has loosened its grip on Burberry, despite ramping up its pursuit of high-fashion names.
The retail giant, which owns Sports Direct and Flannels, had built up a position in Burberry over recent weeks but has now faltered in its pursuit of the group.
Frasers Group had increased its position in Burberry up to 7.4 per cent as recently as last week. The stake is held through put options, meaning that Frasers has the right to sell them at a fixed price.
But Mike Ashley looks to have begun his retreat from the FTSE 100 fashion house, with recent filings showing Frasers’ position in the group was slimmed down to six per cent.
Burberry is worth more than £3.8bn, meaning Frasers Group’s holding in the company is still worth about £240m. Ashley’s firm first took a 4.2 per cent stake in the group in July.
The British fashion house is in the midst of a turnaround under chief executive Joshua Schulman, who is attempting to reposition the group in the mid-market after a short-lived foray into ultra-high fashion.
The group has cut thousands of jobs in recent years but has more recently shown signs of recovery, posting a five per cent jump in revenue in the three months to July.
Ashley’s pursuit of Burberry has been part of the retail tycoon’s attempts to push his fashion empire upmarket in recent months.
These efforts had been endorsed by Schulman, who recently praised Flannels for “bring[ing] the energy of a fashion capital to key regional cities, giving more customers the opportunity to buy a Burberry trench coat in their home town”.
Frasers Group bought luxury department store chain Harvey Nichols out of administration for £40m earlier this year, and has said it will use its new acquisition to scale up its Flannels brand.
The retail group has also been in pursuit of Hugo Boss. It holds about 48 per cent of the German fashion house and has told shareholders it wants majority control of the group.
Last month Michael Murray, Frasers’s chief executive and Ashley’s son-in-law, was appointed chairman of Hugo Boss’ supervisory board after its previous boss stepped away due to “recent changes in the company’s shareholder structure”.
Frasers had been tightening its grip on Hugo Boss over the summer, hoovering up positions in the company directly from shareholders after the group slapped down its “inadequate” takeover proposal.

items.title: New West End Company CEO: Healey’s Budget must give High Streets room to grow
items.summary: The West End supports more than 350,000 jobs, attracts visitors from across the world and generates significant economic activity and tax revenue for the wider UK. If the cost of operating here continues to rise, the consequences will be felt well beyond London, says Dee Corsi Two years of Autumn Budgets have heaped costs on [...]
items.body:
New West End Company CEO: Healey’s Budget must give High Streets room to grow
The West End supports more than 350,000 jobs, attracts visitors from across the world and generates significant economic activity and tax revenue for the wider UK. If the cost of operating here continues to rise, the consequences will be felt well beyond London, says Dee Corsi
Two years of Autumn Budgets have heaped costs on to our flagship high street retailers – but could the third time be the charm? John Lewis and M&S, two of the most important brands in the West End, have made their cases publicly that they cannot absorb any further business rate hikes, and there’s signs that government might finally be listening, particularly following recent reports of proposed changes to online retail VAT collection to provide funds to reduce high street business rates.
This is about more than the fortunes of individual retailers. The West End supports more than 350,000 jobs, attracts visitors from across the world and generates significant economic activity and tax revenue for the wider UK. If the cost of operating here continues to rise, the consequences will be felt well beyond London.
Timing is critical. In a recent survey of New West End Company’s members, 75 per cent of respondents said business rates were the biggest or one of the biggest challenges affecting their business. The Autumn Budget must respond to that warning.
From 1st April this year, the higher business rates multiplier came into force and its impact on the West End is no longer a projection but a reality being felt all the way from the boardroom to the high street. The West End now has 335 stores that sit above the £500,000 rateable value threshold. Their combined annual rates liability has jumped from £212m to £274m, representing an average increase of around £183,000 per property. These eye-watering sums are shaping current business decisions to invest, hire or grow in our capital.
Even for businesses on Oxford Street and Regent Street whose rateable values have not materially increased, they have still seen bills rise by around 20 per cent following the expiry of previous reliefs for retail, hospitality and leisure businesses earlier this year. That relief was also capped at £110,000 per business, which means that multi-site operators which anchor high streets across the country received the least protection and now face the largest exposure.
This is all on top of an additional £2.3bn annual cost to the retail sector from increased employer national insurance contributions, successive above-inflation rises in the National Living Wage, and new obligations introduced through the Employment Rights Act. This is not a single tax problem but a cumulative cost base that is becoming unworkable for many businesses.
What our members say
The evidence from our members could not be clearer. We heard from a selection of the West End’s largest retailers representing over 1.6m sq ft of retail space, and a number of property owners, which re-emphasised that business rates are a dominant concern. Every single business said the current rates environment would affect their business, 60 per cent have seen their rates bills rise by more than 10 per cent and 25 per cent have seen rates bills rise by more than 20 per cent.
The consequences are predictable and already unfolding, as rising rates suppress recruitment and investment, businesses are far more likely to delay growth than absorb costs they cannot pass on. The West End is the first-choice destination for millions of domestic and international tourists seeking world-class retail, leisure and entertainment in London, as reflected in our recent global benchmark report, Unlocking The London Advantage, but its global position is at risk without a tax environment to support its growth.
Calling for reform
The Autumn Budget is an opportunity for Andy Burnham’s government to understand what is at stake for retail, for high streets and the wider ecosystem that depends on them.
Firstly, in the short-term, we need to see a freeze to the higher multiplier immediately, with no increases to the so-called “warehouse tax” which disproportionately impacts flagship destinations including the West End. Second, and more medium term, movement from a slab-based to a slice-based multiplier system would mean that liability rises progressively rather than at damaging cliff edges, removing arbitrary limits on business that are detrimental to growth. And, finally, we need to see a longer term approach to the current three-year business rates review cycle to give businesses the long-term certainty they need to plan investments that typically span ten to twenty years.
Businesses in the West End and beyond deserve a rates system that is fair, proportionate and fit for purpose. The Budget is the moment to deliver it.
By Dee Corsi, Chief Executive, New West End Company

items.body:
Post-purchase intelligence platform Narvar announces the return of founder Amit Sharma as CEO
Retail intelligence specialist Narvar is welcoming its founder Amit Sharma back as CEO. Sharma stepped down from the position and moved to an advisory role in 2024, with Anisa Kumar taking on head honcho duties. Kumar joined the San Francisco-based company in late 2021 as Chief Customer Officer.
A spokesperson for Narvar says: “Amit founded Narvar in 2012 with a vision to transform how retailers connect with customers after the sale. Under his leadership, Narvar helped establish the post-purchase category and grew into a trusted partner to more than 1,500 brands and retailers.”
“He returns at a pivotal moment for retail, as AI reshapes how consumers discover, evaluate and purchase products. With deep expertise in the industry and firsthand knowledge of the challenges retailers face, Amit will lead the company into its next chapter, building on the trust, technology and product innovations that have defined it from the start. We thank Anisa Kumar for her leadership and contributions over the past five years and wish her continued success.”
“I'm excited to be back leading Narvar and grateful for the opportunity to build on what we started together more than a decade ago,” says Sharma. “When I founded Narvar, we saw an opportunity to transform the relationship between retailers and their customers by making the experience after checkout just as important as the purchase itself. Today, as AI begins to change how people shop, I see even bigger opportunity to help brands and retailers navigate what's next.”
He adds: “We've spent years earning the trust of some of the world's leading brands, and that trust is something I value enormously. I'm looking forward to spending time with our team, listening to our customers and working together with our key partners to shape the retail industry's next chapter. More to come!”
Narvar did not respond to our request for comment regarding Kumar’s position at the company moving forward.

items.title: Sainsbury’s hopes to regain narrative after Morrisons merger bombshell
items.summary: Sainsbury’s is set to update the market on its latest numbers this week. But the City has one thing in mind: merger talks with Morrisons, writes Felix Armstrong As Sainsbury’s boss Simon Roberts gears up to face the market later this week, business hacks will be getting used to the usual riposte: no comment.  The [...]
items.body:
Sainsbury’s hopes to regain narrative after Morrisons merger bombshell
Sainsbury’s is set to update the market on its latest numbers this week. But the City has one thing in mind: merger talks with Morrisons, writes Felix Armstrong
As Sainsbury’s boss Simon Roberts gears up to face the market later this week, business hacks will be getting used to the usual riposte: no comment.
The one thing the grocery chief executive is desperate to swerve is the main point he’ll be quizzed on: why his supermarket walked away from merger talks with Morrisons and whether it can rule out going back to them.
Sainsbury’s has been making steady market share gains, cementing its position as the UK’s second biggest supermarket chain, far beyond the reach of discounters Lidl and Aldi as they put pressure on Morrisons and Asda.
The orange-liveried grocer has been putting on decent share gains too, adding 20 per cent to its market value across the last five years. The stock has performed especially well this month, putting on five per cent to approach its highest level in a year.
Since Roberts became Sainsbury’s boss in June 2020 he has sought to drive a relentless focus on the company’s food offering. A few months after he took the reins, the grocer announced 420 Argos store closures.
Sainsbury’s completed its retreat from the click-and-collect retailer in July this year, when it was sold to Swift Partners, a newly-formed group of retail experts for £120m – a fraction of the £1.4bn it paid for it.
“Having rebuilt the core strengths of our food business, this agreement allows us to focus all our resources and investment on the significant opportunities ahead,” Roberts said at the time.
The grocer has also withdrawn from its cafe operations under Roberts, shutting all its in-store outlets in January last year, to the tune of more than 3,000 job losses.
Sainsbury’s finds market share gains ‘expensive’
Months ago, the Sainsbury’s boss would have earmarked this Thursday’s first-half results as an opportunity to talk up the supermarket’s efforts to cut the fat and focus on its food aisles.
But this was made impossible when it emerged earlier this month that Sainsbury’s had held talks with Morrisons, its smaller rival, over a potential merger.
This new grocery conglomerate would have put fresh pressure on Tesco’s market dominance and marked the biggest sector shake-up since Sainsbury’s failed takeover of Asda in 2019.
A potential merger with Morrisons could fuel Roberts’ push towards food, industry experts have said. One of Morrisons’ major assets is its in-house manufacturing arm, Myton Food Group.
“Winning market share organically is becoming increasingly difficult and expensive,” said Retail Economics analyst Nicholas Found. “Acquiring Morrisons would deliver an immediate leap in scale, strengthen its food manufacturing capabilities and expand its convenience footprint – narrowing the gap with Tesco.”
But this was not to be, at least for now. The bigger supermarket decided to ditch the discussions in February this year following a disagreement over price, the Financial Times reported.
Roberts will face a barrage of questions on Thursday about why Sainsbury’s felt the need to explore such a takeover, given its relatively steady share price and solid position in the UK’s grocery market.
Richard Hyman, an independent retail analyst, argued City AM that the talks were more likely an “opportunistic” play by Clayton, Dubilier & Rice – Morrisons’s private equity owners – than a proactive effort from Sainsbury’s.
“[Sainsbury’s] holds all the cards. This isn’t necessarily the end of the story, but I very much doubt that Sainsburys will say anything about it at all or want to discuss it,” he said.
The merger talks, whether or not they are revived, indicate that consolidation in the grocery sector is far more feasible than it was seven years ago, when Sainsbury’s takeover of Asda was blocked over fears it would reduce competition.
Food inflation looms
Some industry insiders believe the emergence of Aldi and Lidl as serious competitors to Morrisons and Asda means the UK’s competition watchdog would be far less likely to bat an eyelid if another deal was on the cards today.
Just as Roberts will not be keen to spill the beans on Sainsbury’s’ talks with Morrisons, neither was Ken Murphy, the boss of rival grocer Tesco.
Quizzed on the news earlier this month, he said: “I spend nearly all my time thinking about what’s right for Tesco customers and the Tesco brand, and how we can keep growing this business, irrespective of what’s going on externally. Because at the end of the day, we can only control the controllables.”
Though Tesco, which is sitting on a commanding 27.8 per cent share of the UK’s grocery market, is untroubled by the prospect of a Sainsbury’s merger, it will be on the lookout for its rivals’ comments on food inflation.
The surging energy and supply chain costs caused by the Iran war are expected to put pressure on food prices, with industry figures expecting prices to rise by as much as six per cent year-on-year by July.
Earlier this year, Roberts said food inflation had not been as bad as it had been feared but he will be keen to prove that Sainsbury’s is competing with its rivals to keep a lid on prices.
After Tesco declared itself the UK’s “cheapest full-line grocer” a few weeks ago, its longstanding rival will be keen to prove that it doesn’t need Morrisons to keep up.

items.body:
Quorso and VoCoVo among 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Best Retailer/Tech Supplier Relationship finalists
We’re pleased to announce the shortlist for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Best Retailer/Technology Supplier Relationship category. We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector.
Check out a rundown of our 2026 shortlists and finalists here.
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! It’s now over to our star studded judging panel who will decide the winners to be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.
Click here to book your place at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony on Wednesday, 4th November.
Our 2026 Best Retailer/Technology Supplier Relationship finalists as follows:
Asda and Evolve
Evolve is powering connectivity across more than 10,000 sites for some of the UK’s biggest multi-site brands, including Home Bargains, Pret A Manger and Asda.
Most managed network providers rely on single carrier, generic network designs and reactive support which leaves businesses exposed when outages occur. Evolve challenges this with a carrier-agnostic model that draws on ten alternative providers to ensure speed, resilience and reliability. Its UK-based, round the clock support and nationwide field engineering team deliver a proactive and preventative approach, with 86% of connectivity problems identified before customers experience an issue.
Asda and Deliverect
Deliverect has partnered with Asda Express to simplify on-demand retail operations across its estate, consolidating separate Uber Eats, Deliveroo and Just Eat picking workflows into one unified application.
Rolled out across the Asda Express estate, the technology gives store teams a single process for managing and picking marketplace orders, reducing operational complexity while significantly improving product availability and picking accuracy. The simpler experience has also driven improved staff NPS. Beyond operational efficiency, the initiative provides the technology infrastructure underpinning Asda Express's q-commerce success, creating a scalable ecosystem where additional digital channels and capabilities can be introduced easily as and when required.
cardfactory, Retail Response and Flooid
cardfactory, Flooid and Retail Response have built a trusted technology partnership spanning almost a decade. Over the past 12 months, this relationship has strengthened through two complex, estate wide technology programmes.
Flooid provided cardfactory with a modernised PoS platform supporting its long-term strategy for personalised customer engagement, streamlined journeys and future omnichannel capabilities. Retail Response delivered the nationwide implementation, visiting over 1,100 stores twice, over two eight-week spans, to deploy the new PoS and subsequently the integrated payments solution.
The partnership extends into long-term support, combining Flooid’s service desk with Retail Response’s field engineering and logistics capabilities to provide cardfactory with a joined-up, resilient technology service.
Dunelm and VoCoVo
Since 2019, Dunelm and VoCoVo have built a collaborative partnership that has evolved from improving in-store communication to driving a digitally led transformation across almost 200 stores. Initially replacing inefficient walkie talkies, facilitating fluid communication, and improving colleague safety, the relationship between Dunelm and VoCoVo has grown to support operational changes.
Within the last 12 months, Dunelm has begun upgrading to VoCoVo’s Series 5 Pro Headsets, creating a connected operational platform that directly addresses core retail challenges. This upgrade has enhanced day-to-day reliability while unlocking AI powered features and real-time operational alerts that change the way colleagues handle and respond to customer queries.
East of England Co-op and Transaction Network Services (TNS)
East of England Co-op engaged Transaction Network Services (TNS) after experiencing fragmented service and slow responsiveness from its previous network provider. The resulting partnership has delivered a fully managed TNS Secure SD-WAN platform across more than 200 sites; the technology delivered results, but the strong relationship between TNS and its customer made the difference.
Named account management, dedicated project leadership and proactive communication replaced a multi-divisional provider experience with one accountable team. Through a close and trusted supplier relationship, East of England Co-op benefits from a partner that understands its business, communicates proactively and provides consistent, human support, underpinning confidence in both daily operations and long-term growth.
H&M and TCS
H&M partnered with TCS to redesign retail operations around an AI first, predictive model that reshapes operations beyond traditional monitoring. The solution combines unified data, contextual intelligence and agentic automation to make operations smarter and business-aware across stores, supply chain and production.
Operating across 4,200 stores in 79 markets, Agentic AI acts as first responder, detecting anomalies, assessing business impact and enabling proactive action, delivering reduced major incidents, improved BOPIS performance, stabilised peak trading and cost savings, showing how emerging technologies can move beyond pilots to deliver scalable, real‑world value across omnichannel retail, accelerating organisation towards Brand Plan goals.
Matalan and Toshiba Global Commerce Solutions
Matalan and Toshiba Global Commerce Solutions partnered to transform the retailer's in-store technology estate and create a platform for future omnichannel innovation. Following a six-month RFP process, the organisations evolved a long-standing supplier relationship into a strategic partnership focused on customer convenience, colleague experience and operational agility.
Together, they deployed Toshiba's VisualStore Commerce Platform and upgraded 1,648 tills across 217 stores. The initiative increased Express Checkout adoption, improved reliability and accelerated innovation. It also established a scalable foundation for future loyalty, personalisation and omnichannel capabilities that will support Matalan's long-term transformation ambitions.
The Fresh Market and Vusion
The Fresh Market and Vusion continue to build a strategic partnership that extends well beyond technology deployment. Together, the companies are transforming The Fresh Market’s stores into connected retail environments that improve pricing accuracy, shelf visibility, associate workflows and guest experience.
The relationship began with a major Connected Store roll-out across The Fresh Market’s US store fleet, including electronic shelf labels, VusionCloud, Captana Computer Vision & AI and Memory Store Analytics, marking the first Vusion 360 rollout in North America. Since then, the partnership evolved into a deeper collaboration focused on operational design, associate adoption, measurable performance improvement and public education around how connected store technology can support hospitality led grocery retail.
TRIP and GoPlaces
TRIP was the number one drinks brand on TikTok Shop in 2025. GoPlaces believes that achievement was a result of a brand and its agency that stopped behaving like client and agency. TRIP shared commercially sensitive performance history and worked alongside its engineers; GoPlaces built technology, OnePlace, around the problems that data exposed and ran a professional LIVE commerce operation on top.
The predictive creator scoring engine now serving 22 brands exists because TRIP went first. In 90 days ROAS rose 57% and wasted media fell 42%. Over 12 months, TRIP outsold Heineken in Dry January. This is the commercial impact of a partnership that built the product.
Yours Clothing and Poq
Yours Clothing and poq’s partnership has gone from strength to strength since 2018, with the last 12 months being the most ambitious yet. Building on a group wide roll-out that already spans M&Co, Evans, Bad Rhino, Long Tall Sally and Pixie Girl, the partnership has now gone global.
As the first phase of international expansion, the Yours Clothing app has taken a proven UK model into new markets, currencies and languages for the first time, with more to come. Rather than slowing as the group has grown, the relationship has sped up: each new market launch draws on lessons from the last, with poq and Yours Clothing's teams working from a shared, evolving playbook rather than starting from scratch each time.

Our 2026 Hospitality Technology Innovation finalists as follows:
atis
In spring, atis launched its first customer app, built entirely in-house over 18 months on proprietary technology. Bringing Click and Collect, loyalty and rewards into one place through atis Insiders, the app was designed to create a more seamless customer journey while giving atis greater ownership of its digital channel.
Bar Tap, Wembley Stadium
Bar Tap Wembley boosts live event hospitality by removing one of its biggest barriers to customer satisfaction and spend, queuing.
Powered by Amazon’s Just Walk Out technology, it creates a fast, frictionless food and drink experience designed for Wembley’s high footfall environment. The guiding principle is simple, customers experience the benefit, not the technology. Sophisticated technology works quietly behind the scenes, making purchasing feel effortless.
Combining frictionless payment, automated technology and real-time operational data, Bar Tap increases throughput and operator control. Its modular, recyclable construction provides a scalable platform for future deployment, while proven sales uplift demonstrates measurable commercial impact.
Gonzo's Tea Room and Epos Now
Gonzo's Tea Room in Norwich has grown from a single ground floor bar in 2014 into a four-floor, award winning venue with multiple bars, dance floors, a rooftop cocktail bar and food concepts Brix and Bones and Voodoo Daddy's Pizza.
Epos Now has powered every stage: one integrated PoS, payments and Multi-Site Manager platform connecting every bar, till and team member. Gonzo's uses Epos Now data not only for stock and pricing but to shape the guest experience, deciding on DJs, sound and lighting. The result is a scalable, data led venue named BBC Radio 1's Best Venue in Europe.
NomNom
NomNom is a commission free booking and table management system built for independent restaurants, pubs and cafes. Guests book on the venue's own branded page instead of a marketplace, so the venue keeps every cover, owns its guest data and takes its own deposits.
Staff run the diary, table plan and guest profiles in any desktop browser or on iOS and Android, while automated SMS reminders and card holds cut no-shows. It replaced e-Res, the system its team ran for 25 years, and costs one flat monthly fee per venue, with no contract, setup fee or sales call.
TARA by Net0link AI
TARA by Net0link AI helps hotels improve cooling performance through operating intelligence rather than starting with equipment replacement. Net0link reports a 31.3% efficiency improvement at an IHCL hotel in Delhi and an average improvement of 27.5%.
Current work spans 28 hotel facilities: 18 in India, 5 in Singapore and 5 in Dubai, representing approximately 14 million square feet and 33,600 TR of cooling capacity. A separate engagement covers an Emirates lounge at Dubai International Airport. TARA's proposition combines better asset utilisation, operator oversight and measurable performance, creating a repeatable route towards lower cooling costs and associated emissions across international hospitality.

Westfield Rise and Lionsgate launch Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping immersive experience in London
Westfield Rise, the in-house retail media agency of Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield (URW), has partnered with Lionsgate to launch The Hunger Games: The Capitol Experience, an exclusive immersive activation at Westfield London. Running from 30th October to 23rd November, the free ticketed experience will give fans the chance to step into the world of Panem ahead of the release of the movie.
Located in The Atrium at Westfield London, it will feature a Cornucopia installation, interactive moments inspired by the film, exclusive collectibles and a world exclusive film clip available only to visitors attending the activation. The activation forms part of Lionsgate’s wider campaign for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, which the studio has described as its largest above the line campaign of 2026, spanning TV, VOD, outdoor, social, digital, radio, PR, influencer and brand partnership activity.
Westfield will support the campaign through its owned marketing channels, including social media, CRM, digital platforms, editorial content, in-centre media and ticketing communications. The partnership also extends across URW's Northern European portfolio. Supporting activity at Westfield Täby Centrum and Westfield Mall of the Netherlands will help amplify the campaign through local marketing, social content and customer communications. Additional campaign activity will also take place at Westfield Chodov in Prague.
“The Hunger Games is one of the world's most recognisable entertainment franchises, with a fanbase that actively wants to engage with the story beyond the screen. Westfield London provides the stage for a standout fan experience, while activity across our destinations in Sweden and the Netherlands helps build excitement for the film across Northern Europe,” says Mel Lalou, Director at Westfield Rise, Northern Europe.
“For us, it's a strong example of how we help brands extend campaigns beyond a single activation through the reach of our destinations and marketing channels. Westfield Rise offered the ideal combination of destination scale, creativity and marketing reach. Together, we’re creating an experience that fans will want to visit, share and talk about while building excitement for the film across key markets in Northern Europe.”

items.body:
Sephoria London was a brilliant day out, but did paying beauty fans get what they were promised?
RTIH's Secret Shopper heads to the first UK SEPHORiA and finds brilliant vibes, big queues and a beauty event that did not always live up to the hype.
SEPHORiA London is going to be a slightly awkward review to write because Secret Shopper Bestie and I had a brilliant time. The atmosphere was fantastic, the venue looked amazing, we discovered products we now want to buy and came home with a very respectable amount of beauty loot. Step away from our own day, though, and look at the event as a £95 experience for paying Sephora customers, and there is quite a lot to unpick.
For anyone who has somehow missed the SEPHORiA phenomenon, it is essentially Sephora turned into a beauty festival: brands, new products, masterclasses, games, makeovers, activations and the now-famous goody bags all packed into one event. It first launched in Los Angeles in 2018 and has since grown into an international format, building a fairly legendary reputation among beauty fans along the way, particularly because of the huge hauls that come out of the US editions. London marked the first time SEPHORiA had landed in the UK, so there was a lot riding on whether the British version could live up to what we had all been watching online for years.
Demand was ridiculous. Tickets disappeared almost instantly, with several three-hour sessions running across Friday and Saturday, plus an exclusive Gold member session.
Annoyingly, when tickets went on sale, I was 86 points away from Gold status. Eighty-six points between me and that Gold session was particularly painful, although I am happy to report that I have now finally made it, so next year I will be watching that ticket release very closely.
For this one, though, I joined the general ticket scramble, paid £95 and attended the Saturday 12pm to 3pm session with Secret Shopper Bestie. There was no press invite, no special access and nobody at the event knew I was reviewing it, so everything that follows is based on the same experience any other paying customer could have had.
Given my long-standing Sephora obsession, expectations were already fairly high, and what we saw coming out of the event before our session pushed them considerably higher.
Influencer night had us expecting beauty Disneyland
The Thursday preview filled TikTok and Instagram with creators, influencers and press wandering around what looked like a beautifully spacious venue. They seemed able to move between brand stands without the enormous queues that would later dominate the public sessions, while showing off some seriously impressive gifts along the way.
There were full-size products, multiple products from individual brands and even fragrances people said had not yet launched. The haul videos afterwards looked incredible and, by the time Secret Shopper Bestie and I headed into London, everything we had seen suggested this was going to be another level.
The paying-customer experience turned out to be much more mixed, although that is not to say people received nothing. We came home with a decent goody bag, picked up products from several brands and found plenty of things worth talking about afterwards, but there was a noticeable difference between what had been shown online and what many customers actually encountered once the public sessions began.
At some stands, where preview attendees had appeared to receive full-size products, paying visitors were given minis or tiny samples. Other brands required customers to win a game before receiving anything substantial, while some handed out the sort of product you might normally expect to receive free with an online beauty order.
Marc Jacobs became one of the more surreal examples discussed online after attendees reported queueing only to receive a pencil sharpener. Some Fenty visitors thought they had been given a mini product before opening the packaging and finding sweets inside. None of that would necessarily be outrageous at a free event, but at £95 a ticket, after watching the influencer preview the night before, it inevitably lands differently.
Did SEPHORiA actually need influencers to sell SEPHORiA?
The influencer conversation is probably one of the most interesting parts of the whole event because I do not think the answer is simply that Sephora should stop inviting influencers. Creators are part of beauty marketing, brands give them products in return for content and exposure, and there is nothing particularly unusual about holding a preview for press and creators before a consumer event opens.
But SEPHORiA had already sold out, with people desperate for tickets before influencer night had even taken place. Sephora did not particularly need creators to persuade customers to attend because there were no tickets left to sell.
What it did have was thousands of extremely enthusiastic paying beauty fans who were about to create their own content whether Sephora had asked them to or not. That is where the strategy starts to look a little like an own goal, because those customers could have become some of the event’s most persuasive advertising.
Had they walked out feeling completely spoilt, talking about brilliant products, easy access to brands and an event that exceeded expectations, TikTok would have done the rest. Hundreds of ordinary customers saying, “You have to go next year,” after spending their own money carries a very different sort of weight.
Instead, a lot of the viral content afterwards focused on the difference between influencer night and the public sessions. Even some of the more positive reviews came with caveats about queues, stock, samples or the difference between what creators had received and what paying customers found.
One comment I saw summed it up particularly well, with the attendee saying the products she received probably would have seemed perfectly fine had she not spent the previous day watching influencers show off unreleased and full-size products online. The public event did not suddenly become bad because influencers received more, but the preview had effectively become the advertisement for an experience many customers then felt they did not receive.
Three hours goes very quickly when you are queueing for everything
Once inside, the biggest practical issue was obvious: the queues. Secret Shopper Bestie and I had gone in with a plan, with brands we definitely wanted to visit, others we would try if the queue looked sensible and a few we were prepared to sacrifice if necessary.
Even with that strategy, there was no chance of seeing everything. YSL was one of the casualties because the queue seemed permanently enormous, and after checking back a couple of times we eventually accepted that it simply was not going to happen.
Online, plenty of other attendees had similar stories. Some said they waited 30 or 40 minutes only to be turned away because an activation was ending, while others reported queues being closed well before the end of their ticketed session.
People attending later on Saturday also complained that some stands had already run low on products or run out entirely. One attendee said brands were already running short during our 12pm to 3pm session and felt sorry for anyone coming afterwards, while visitors to later slots posted about finding certain products gone very early into their own session.
That is something Sephora needs to look at very carefully next year because everybody has paid for the same event. Someone entering during the final session should not feel as though they have bought access to whatever happens to be left after earlier groups have gone home.
There were also complaints about queue management and security, with some attendees saying they were prevented from joining lines 40 minutes or more before closing. Experiences clearly varied, but the same themes appeared often enough online that they are difficult to dismiss as isolated bad luck.
Hourglass proved why the whole concept can work brilliantly
Ironically, one of the longest queues we did join resulted in one of my favourite parts of the day. Hourglass was busy and only a small number of people appeared to be working on the stand, while the activation itself involved actually having some makeup applied rather than simply collecting something and moving on.
On a three-hour ticket, that setup could easily become frustrating, but the woman who looked after me was fantastic. She applied one of the Hourglass blush and highlighter palettes, talked me through what she was doing and made it look so good that I immediately decided I needed it, so Mr Secret Shopper should consider this his warning that the Christmas list is incoming.
That activation did exactly what these events should do. Hourglass did not just put a free product into my hand; the team got the makeup onto my face, showed me why I might want it and almost certainly secured a future sale as a result. We also came away with a lovely travel-sized Hourglass gift, so there was something tangible to keep trying at home rather than the experience ending the moment we left the stand.
The only issue is how that type of interaction scales when every person needs several minutes with a member of staff and only a handful of people are working on the stand. Next year, I would love to see those longer consultations made optional, allowing customers who want the full experience to have one while people who already know the brand or simply want a quicker introduction can move through at a faster pace.
Plenty of brand teams absolutely nailed it
It would be unfair to make SEPHORiA sound as though every stand was chaotic or disappointing because that was not our experience at all. Makeup by Mario was great, Summer Fridays was great, Erborian had staff who were happy to talk properly about the products and Sephora’s own team were friendly and enthusiastic.
Hourglass, as mentioned, sold me something I had not even planned to buy, which is probably the ultimate compliment at a beauty event. Most of the people we dealt with were warm, knowledgeable and clearly happy to be there.
Glowery deserves a particular mention too. It was one of the brands that seemed to build real momentum during the public sessions, with its quick grab-style activation and worthwhile products being talked about online afterwards. That is exactly the sort of organic reaction I mean when I talk about paying customers becoming the marketing: people discovered the brand at SEPHORiA, liked what it was doing and started telling everybody else to go there.
Charlotte Tilbury was more mixed. Two women working on the stand continued talking to one another when I approached and did not acknowledge me, which was disappointing, but the man who eventually helped me was lovely and could not have been more helpful.
Interestingly, the online comments showed just how inconsistent those individual experiences could be. Other attendees praised Charlotte Tilbury staff and said they had received plenty of samples, while completely different opinions appeared about other brands depending on the session.
That probably explains some of the polarised reaction to SEPHORiA. There was no single version of the day because your three hours depended heavily on your time slot, which queues you chose, what stock was left and even which person happened to be standing behind the counter when you arrived.
Let the games be fun, not another hurdle
I am very pro silly beauty game, so give me a wheel to spin, something to grab, a button to press or some ridiculous challenge and Secret Shopper will probably participate. The problem comes when a fun activation becomes another barrier between the customer and the product.
At some stands, people needed to queue, take part in a game and then win before receiving anything substantial. Elsewhere, several minutes of product education or activity were effectively compulsory before you could move on.
That works brilliantly if you have all afternoon, but it is much harder to justify when the ticket gives you three hours and dozens of brands are competing for the same limited time. Games should make the experience more entertaining rather than becoming another reason a queue stops moving.
Glowery was a good example of getting the balance right. Its activation was quick, there was something worthwhile at the end of it and word spread, which meant a brand that had been much less familiar to some attendees suddenly had people actively seeking it out.
The people paying to attend SEPHORiA are already highly engaged beauty customers. Give them something exciting to take home, let them try it properly and there is every chance that a free product becomes a future purchase.
The vibes, though? Immaculate
For all the criticisms, the atmosphere was probably my favourite part of the whole event. Secret Shopper Bestie and I compared it to being at Taylor Swift, not because anybody suddenly launched into All Too Well beside the Rare Beauty stand, but because there was that same feeling of being surrounded by people who were all extremely excited about the same thing.
There were groups of friends, mums and daughters, couples, younger beauty fans, older beauty fans and people from all sorts of backgrounds. It felt inclusive, happy and very welcoming, which is something SEPHORiA absolutely deserves credit for.
Despite the monster queues, nobody around us was pushing, snapping or arguing. People chatted to strangers, compared what they had picked up and told each other which stands were worth visiting, which gave the whole event a very friendly atmosphere even when everyone was watching the clock.
The venue itself looked fantastic too. The London theme worked, the different areas made it feel like an actual experience rather than a trade show, and everything had been designed to photograph well without feeling completely soulless. For atmosphere alone, SEPHORiA gets five stars from me, and whatever else needs work next year, I would not want Sephora to lose that feeling.
Masterclasses versus three precious hours
There were also masterclasses, and by all accounts some of them were excellent, but we did not do any. It was not through lack of interest; the problem was simply how much of our limited session one would consume.
If you are encouraged to arrive around half an hour before a half-hour class, that can take up roughly a third of a three-hour ticket. When Hourglass, YSL, Makeup by Mario, Rare Beauty and dozens of other stands are all competing for those same three hours, it becomes very hard to justify.
A longer session would change that completely. At the moment, attendees are effectively forced to choose between doing the programmed content properly and getting around enough of the brand activations.
Food, drink and somewhere to sit would not go amiss
Food and refreshments were fairly limited too, with a matcha bar that was excellent news if you happen to love matcha. Punchy was also handing out its hydration drinks, and this was one of those smaller bits of product discovery that worked on me immediately because Secret Shopper Bestie and I enjoyed them enough to go back for another.
They also came home in the haul, alongside Jimmy’s Iced Coffee, and Punchy is now firmly a brand I would buy again. That is another very simple example of why giving people something useful to try can be more effective than overcomplicating an activation.
Beyond that, there was not a huge amount in the way of food and drink. To be fair, nobody wants to spend half of SEPHORiA queueing for lunch, but a little more food, water and obvious seating would make the event easier, particularly for anyone who cannot comfortably stand for several hours.
There were areas where people could take a break and a wellbeing element for visitors finding the busy environment overwhelming, which was a really positive inclusion. Next time, I would simply make those quieter seated spaces even more obvious and plentiful.
My goody bag was good, but Secret Shopper Bestie’s was completely different
Now to the part everybody wants to know about: the goody bag. Mine was good, with products I was very happy to receive, things I wanted to try and enough in there that I did not come home feeling £95 poorer and furious.
There were some really nice products mixed through it too. Mine included Shiseido Ultimune Power Infusing Serum, a full 30ml bottle of Le Monde Gourmand Fleur de Blonde, Olaplex haircare, Aestura skincare and products from the likes of Summer Fridays, Glow Recipe, Makeup by Mario, Hourglass and Sephora Collection. There were plenty of minis, but there were also products substantial enough to actually use for a meaningful period rather than one application before throwing the sachet away.
Secret Shopper Bestie and I then emptied our bags and realised they were completely different. Her haul included Huda Beauty, Saie, Fenty Beauty, Laneige, Hourglass, Natasha Denona and plenty more, and suddenly the fun surprise element became slightly irritating because we immediately started comparing.
There were things in her bag I would have happily stolen, and vice versa.
That variety is not automatically a bad thing. There is something quite fun about seeing which version you got, and between our two bags there was an impressive spread of brands. The problem comes when some of the differences relate to products people were specifically expecting.
Erborian was particularly frustrating because there was a new product I wanted to test. Someone on the stand told me they were not giving it out there because it would be in the goody bag, so naturally I expected to find it when we got home.
It was not in mine or Secret Shopper Bestie’s, while other people posting online had received it. I can cope with bags containing slightly different products, but if a brand representative tells a customer that something will be waiting for them later, it really needs to be waiting for them later.
Next year, I would also make sure the different versions feel broadly equivalent. They do not need to be identical, but nobody should open TikTok afterwards and feel as though they somehow drew the short straw.
The haul also proves why sampling still works
Going through everything afterwards also softened some of my frustration with the event because there was a lot there that I probably would not have picked up myself.
A Shiseido serum, a Le Monde Gourmand fragrance, products from Aestura and Yepoda, various lip products, skincare and haircare all suddenly became things to test over the following weeks. Even among the smaller items, there were brands I had either never tried or had been meaning to explore.
That is the bit of SEPHORiA brands should lean into much harder.
The point is not necessarily to give everybody the most expensive full-size product on the stand. It is to give people enough of something, or enough of an experience with it, that they actually form an opinion.
A tiny sachet that gets used once may disappear from memory within 24 hours. A decent travel size, an interesting mini or a product someone can properly incorporate into their routine has a much better chance of becoming a sale.
Our haul proves that the model works because there are already products from the event I am planning to keep using, buy in full size or investigate further.
America was always going to be the awkward comparison
SEPHORiA London was never going to escape comparisons with the US events because those enormous American haul videos are part of the reason it has developed the reputation it has. People have watched attendees leave with astonishing amounts of product, and that mythology inevitably follows the event into every new market.
I do not expect a £95 London ticket automatically to come with £1,500 worth of beauty. Different markets, sponsors and event costs exist, so expecting every edition to be identical would be unrealistic.
But Sephora cannot really benefit from the global reputation of SEPHORiA and then expect UK customers not to compare what they receive with the editions they have watched online. Unsurprisingly, that comparison appeared repeatedly after London.
Another comparison came up surprisingly often too: Superdrug Presents. Several commenters said they felt the Superdrug event offered better value, stronger product discovery and more generous sampling for a much lower ticket price, with one even joking that people practically need cabin suitcases for everything they collect there.
That is probably not the comparison Sephora wanted its first UK SEPHORiA to generate. Equally, some attendees did the maths on the value of their goody bags and felt the £95 price was entirely justified, and I can see that argument too.
We got good products, picked up extras at stands and had three hours of entertainment. For me, though, the question was never simply whether the contents of the bag could mathematically add up to £95, but whether the whole event felt like the experience we had been encouraged to expect.
So, was SEPHORiA actually bad?
No, and some of the TikToks describing it as a complete disaster do not reflect the day we had. Secret Shopper Bestie and I had loads of fun, discovered products, met some brilliant brand teams, laughed a lot, came home with plenty of beauty and spent three hours surrounded by people who were just as excited about makeup and skincare as we were.
I would absolutely go again, and there are obvious allowances to make for the fact that this was Sephora’s first attempt at bringing SEPHORiA to the UK. First events have teething problems, and most of what went wrong here feels fixable rather than fundamental.
The next edition needs better queue management and enough stock protected for every session, while brands need clearer expectations around what they are offering and how long their activations take. The influencer preview also needs a little more thought so that it does not accidentally advertise a version of the event that paying customers cannot access.
If demand remains this ridiculous, Sephora should seriously consider a bigger venue, longer sessions, more brands or some combination of all three. More activations would spread people out, give visitors more choice and take pressure off the handful of huge names everybody currently rushes towards at once.
It would also make the three-hour format feel less like a military operation where you and your best friend are comparing queue lengths and abandoning YSL like a failed mission. And yes, I would very much like Sephora to look after its Gold members next year, which I am shamelessly saying now that I have finally joined the club.
SEPHORiA London was not the beauty disaster some social posts made it sound like, but it was not quite the all-access beauty wonderland we had watched influencers enjoying either. For me, it sits somewhere in the middle: a very fun first attempt with immaculate vibes, some excellent brand experiences and enough problems around capacity, stock, consistency and expectation-setting to explain why a noticeable number of loyal Sephora customers came away disappointed.
The audience is already there, and people desperately want SEPHORiA, its tickets, its brands and the whole experience. Next time, Sephora just needs to make sure those paying customers feel like the main event.
Secret Shopper rating: 3 out of 5 stars
Vibes: 5 out of 5 stars

items.body:
Apadmi works with Matalan to build clothing and homewares retailer’s first fully native mobile app
Matalan reports that its first fully native app has recorded 1.76 million downloads since launching in August, with monthly active users growing by 10% month-on-month since go live. App orders increased 20% year-on-year in August and 28% in September, while conversion has reached 4.4%, ahead of its 3.4% target. Average order value is also 14% higher than on Matalan's website.
Developed in partnership with Apadmi, features include intelligent search to help customers find products more easily, richer product content and streamlined checkout through Apple Pay and Google Pay. The app also brings Matalan Me rewards and account information together in one place, making it easier for customers to access their benefits and personalised offers.
It is designed to connect Matalan's digital and physical shopping experiences. An in-store barcode scanning feature allows customers to check product details, availability and reviews using their phones, helping them move more easily between shopping in-store and online.
Dre Nicolaides, Digital Director at Matalan, comments: “What’s particularly encouraging about the response to our new app is that customers aren’t just downloading it - they’re using it to shop, and we’re seeing that translate into stronger orders and conversion. It’s a really positive start and reflects the investment we’ve made in improving the digital experience.”
“We’ve focused on making it easier and more enjoyable to shop Matalan, whether customers are shopping online or checking product information in store. The investment we’ve made in the technology also means we can keep introducing new features and responding more quickly to what customers want. We see significant potential to grow digital at Matalan, and the app will play an important part in that. These early results are encouraging, but we’ve got much more planned.”
Keeley Lee, Client Services Director at Apadmi, says: “We’ve worked closely with the Matalan team to create an app that delivers a better experience for customers and supports the business’s ambitions for digital growth. It’s been a great partnership, and seeing such encouraging early results makes it particularly rewarding. We’re looking forward to continuing our work together.”

items.body:
Former IGD Commercial Customer Director Kate Sizer joins TruRating as its new Chief Customer Officer
TruRating has appointed Kate Sizer, most recently Commercial Customer Director at IGD, as Chief Customer Officer. Sizer will focus on strengthening the company’s enterprise client relationships, helping retailers put customer insights to work across their businesses, and expanding the advisory support that turns those insights into clear priorities.
TruRating asks one anonymous question at payment and links each answer to the purchase. It claims that, on average, 84% of in-store customers answer, giving retailers enough feedback to understand how customer experience impacts commercial outcomes at store and shift level.
Sizer joins as TruRating expands how clients use that data, from configurable dashboards to their own data warehouse and AI assistants their teams already use. She has spent more than 20 years in grocery, working with clients to collect, interpret, and act on customer research and insights.
“Customers are thinking harder about where they shop, and retailers want data they can trust before they hand decisions to AI. As more retailers turn to TruRating, Kate will make sure they act on what they learn, from the store floor to the boardroom. I’m so excited to have her with us,” says Georgina Nelson, CEO and Co-founder at TruRating.
“With customer experiences evolving so quickly, I was drawn to TruRating’s unique ability to capture vast volumes of data as each purchase happens, so problems surface before they cost another customer. As commercial pressures increase, leading with insights that show a clear return is critical for future decision-making,” says Sizer.

items.title: West End boss urges Healey to curb ‘eye-watering’ business rates
items.summary: The West End’s top business chief has urged John Healey to avoid adding to high street firms’ “eye-watering” business rates bills. Writing in City AM, New West End Company chief executive Dee Corsi said the Chancellor must listen to retailers and hospitality businesses who say they “cannot absorb” any more tax hikes.  The industry body, [...]
items.body:
West End boss urges Healey to curb ‘eye-watering’ business rates
The West End’s top business chief has urged John Healey to avoid adding to high street firms’ “eye-watering” business rates bills.
Writing in City AM, New West End Company chief executive Dee Corsi said the Chancellor must listen to retailers and hospitality businesses who say they “cannot absorb” any more tax hikes.
The industry body, which represents more than 800 high street firms, has warned that the West End could lose ground to other global hospitality and shopping districts if its tax burden continues to grow.
Corsi said Healey must break the trend set by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, whose two Budgets “heaped costs onto our flagship high street retailers”.
Business rates are the biggest concern for the West End’s retail and hospitality firms, the trade body chief said. 335 shops in the district were caught by the new business rates multiplier which applies for all premises with a value of £500,000 or higher, she said.
The combined rates bill of these shops has jumped from £212m to £274m, representing an average increase of £183,000 per property.
“These eye-watering sums are shaping current business decisions to invest, hire or grow in the capital,” Corsi said.
End business rates ‘cliff edges,’ Healey told
The New West End Company has urged the Chancellor to freeze the higher business rates multiplier, which it says “disproportionately impacts” flagship stores in areas like Oxford Street.
Earlier this month, HMV said it will close its Oxford Street flagship only three years after returning to the street where it founded its first store. The entertainment retailer blamed a surging rent bill.
The bosses of department store giants John Lewis and Marks & Spencer have urged John Healey to tackle business rates at the Budget later this month.
Corsi also called on the Chancellor to shift to a more gradual business rates system, in which bills “rise progressively rather than at damaging cliff edges”.
Healey should also lengthen the existing three-year business rates review cycle to give business more certainty, she said.
“Businesses in the West End and beyond deserve a rates system that is fair, proportionate and fit for purpose, which can drive growth and protect global investment,” she added.
A Treasury spokesperson said: “The Chancellor is prioritising giving businesses the breathing space to invest, grow and manage cost pressures, which is why we are backing firms through business rates cuts, a cap on corporation tax, and a £4.3bn support package to limit bill rises.
“As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

items.title: Consumer confidence slumps to lowest level in more than three years
items.summary: Cost of living pressures combined with fears of interest rate hikes sent the consumer sentiment index compiled by S&P Global to 41.3 in October from 42.7 in September.
items.body:
Consumer confidence slumps to lowest level in more than three years
Consumer confidence has slumped to its lowest level in more than three years.
Households have become 'increasingly downbeat' ahead of next week's Budget, said experts at S&P Global, which compiles the consumer sentiment index.
Cost-of-living pressures combined with fears of interest rate hikes sent the index to 41.3 in October from 42.7 in September. It was the lowest level since July 2023.
Maryam Baluch, economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said: 'Any 'Burnham bounce' has proved short-lived, eclipsed by the impact on the cost of living from events in the Middle East and the accompanying prospect of higher interest rates.
'October has brought a growing conviction among households that borrowing costs will rise imminently as the Bank of England seeks to tame inflation.
'Households will need to start feeling brighter about their financial prospects and job security than we're seeing in the lead up to the Budget if hopes of stronger growth… are to become anything more than wishful thinking.'

items.body:
Harry Ramsden’s Group is bringing its compact Harry’s Hut format to Frasers Plus Designer Outlet Swindon, opening on Monday 19 October ahead of an official Grand Opening celebration on Friday 23 October.
Harry’s Hut is the brand’s smaller-footprint format, designed to bring the Harry Ramsden’s experience to high-footfall destinations while keeping the quality, craft and signature menu the brand is known for, including hand-battered fish and chips prepared in beef dripping and freshly prepared chips. The name is a deliberate nod to the brand’s origins: Harry Ramsden began serving fish and chips from a ten-foot wooden hut in Guiseley, West Yorkshire, in 1928.
The new site sits within Frasers Plus Designer Outlet Swindon, one of the UK’s leading outlet shopping destinations, housed in the restored Great Western Railway works and home to over 90 designer and high-street brands alongside a line-up of cafés and restaurants. Harry Ramsden’s adds its heritage to the centre’s food and drink offer. The opening follows Harry’s Hut at Tower Bridge in August 2026.
To mark the opening, Harry Ramsden’s will take its signature Fish & Chips back to 1928 prices (7p) for the first 100 customers on Grand Opening Day, as a nod to the original hut. The celebration will also include a Spin the Wheel merchandise giveaway, face painting for children and product sampling, with local partnerships building awareness in the run-up.
Harry Ramsden’s joins a strong and growing line-up of food and drink signings at Frasers Plus Designer Outlet Swindon, as Global Mutual continues to develop a broader, more dynamic offer alongside the outlet’s established retail mix.
The opening forms part of the Group’s plan to grow Harry Ramsden’s across high-traffic, high-visibility locations throughout the UK, whether on the motorway, on the high street, or on the go.
James Fleming, chief executive oficer at Harry Ramsden’s Group said: “Harry’s Hut gives us a way to take Harry Ramsden’s into high-footfall destinations in a compact, flexible format, without compromising on the quality and craft the brand is known for. Frasers Plus Designer Outlet Swindon is the kind of high-footfall destination where the format can really work, and a strong partner to open with. Almost a century on from the original hut in Guiseley, this opening reinforces our ability to adapt and stay relevant.”
Nicky Lovell, head of outlets and retail business development at Global Mutual, said: “Harry Ramsden’s is a strong signing for Frasers Plus Designer Outlet Swindon. It is part of the continued investment and change taking place across the destination, bringing an iconic British brand and a distinctive offer to our food and drink line-up.”
